facts.fact: Where ramp handrails are not continuous between runs, they must extend horizontally at least 12 in beyond the top and bottom of each ramp run.
Door thresholds may be no more than 3/4 in high for sliding doors serving dwelling units and no more than 1/2 in high for other doors.

Accessible car parking spaces must be at least 96 in wide with access aisles at least 60 in wide; where spaces and aisles are marked with lines, widths are measured from the centerline of the markings.
Objects with leading edges between 27 and 80 in above the floor may protrude no more than 4 in horizontally into a circulation path.

Doors in toilet and bathing rooms may swing into the turning space but not into a fixture's clear floor space; in a single-user room, the door may swing into fixture clear floor spaces if a clear floor space of at least 30 x 48 in is provided inside the room beyond the arc of the door swing.
facts.reviewed: 603.2.3 already lets doors swing into the turning space; Exception 2 lets a single-user room door swing into fixture clearances

facts.fact: In a private residence elevator, the clearance between the car platform and the edge of any landing sill may not exceed 1-1/4 in.
Accessible elevator car control buttons and hall call buttons must be at least 3/4 in in their smallest dimension.
Interior swinging doors other than fire doors must open with no more than 5 lbf of push or pull force.
An accessible water closet seat must be 17 to 19 in above the finished floor, measured to the top of the seat.
Accessible ramps may have a running slope of no more than 1:12 and a rise of no more than 30 in per run, so a run at 1:12 can be at most 30 ft long before a landing is needed.
Accessible parking spaces and access aisles may not slope more than 1:48 (about 2 percent) in any direction.
facts.note: Card says 1:45. The ADA Standards and ICC A117.1 limit parking space and access aisle slopes to 1:48.

facts.fact: Escalators provided in below-grade transportation stations must have a clear width of at least 32 in.
The clearance around an accessible water closet must be at least 60 in wide measured perpendicular from the side wall, and at least 56 in deep measured from the rear wall.
When ramp edge protection is provided by an extended floor surface instead of a curb, the ramp surface must extend at least 12 in beyond the inside face of the handrail.
On an accessible route, a change in level up to 1/4 in may be vertical; from 1/4 in to 1/2 in it must be beveled no steeper than 1:2; anything over 1/2 in must be ramped.
Accessible routes can be made up of walking surfaces with a running slope no steeper than 1:20, doorways, ramps, curb ramps (not counting flared sides), elevators and platform lifts.
A van-accessible parking space must be at least 132 in wide with a 60-in access aisle, or 96 in wide when the adjacent access aisle is at least 96 in wide.

Accessible washing machines need a clear floor space for a parallel approach centered on the appliance, and for front-loading machines one standard is cited as allowing the space's centerline to be offset up to 24 in from the door centerline.
facts.note: Card says 24 in maximum offset from the door centerline. ADA 611 centers the space on the appliance; the 24-in offset appears to come from an ICC A117.1 dwelling-unit provision that I could not confirm.

facts.fact: A ramp run with a rise greater than 6 in must have handrails on both sides, and handrails with a circular cross section must have an outside diameter of 1-1/4 in to 2 in.

In a wheelchair-accessible toilet compartment, the door goes in the front partition or the side wall farthest from the water closet; if it is in the front partition, the opening must be no more than 4 in from the side wall farthest from the toilet.
Accessible operable parts must work with one hand, without tight grasping, pinching or twisting of the wrist, and with no more than 5 lbf of force.
Accessible ramps may have a running slope no steeper than 1:12, and the cross slope of ramp runs and landings may be no steeper than 1:48, which still lets water drain without pooling.
For wheelchair users, a drinking fountain spout outlet may be no higher than 36 in above the floor; standing-person fountains have spouts 38 to 43 in high.
Manual control switches for automatic doors and gates must meet the operable-parts rules, and their clear floor space must be beyond the arc of the door swing.
A handrail mounted next to a wall or other surface must have a clear space of at least 1-1/2 in between the handrail and the wall.
When no soil investigation is done, the presumptive allowable bearing pressure for clay, sandy clay, silty clay, clayey silt and silt (CL, ML, MH, CH) is 1,500 psf.

Presumptive allowable foundation pressures: crystalline bedrock 12,000 psf; sedimentary and foliated rock 4,000 psf; sandy gravel and gravel (GW, GP) 3,000 psf; sand, silty or clayey sand and silty or clayey gravel 2,000 psf; clays and silts 1,500 psf.
Commercial kitchens use an occupant load factor of 200 gross sq ft per occupant. A 42 ft x 70 ft kitchen (2,940 sq ft) works out to 14.7, which is rounded up to 15 occupants.
facts.note: Card answers 14, which truncates 14.7. Fractional occupant loads are rounded up in design practice (ICC commentary), giving 15. The 200 gross factor itself is correct.

facts.fact: A shear wall is a wall designed to resist lateral forces (wind or seismic) acting parallel to the plane of the wall.
Copper water tube is color coded by wall thickness: Type K (thickest) green, Type L blue, Type M (thinnest) red.

Walls, partitions and floor-ceiling assemblies separating dwelling or sleeping units from each other or from public areas must have an STC of at least 50 (45 if field tested); floor-ceiling assemblies also need an IIC of at least 50 (45 field tested).
A three-phase panel has three ungrounded (hot) phase legs, A, B and C; a three-phase four-wire service adds a grounded neutral conductor to those three phases.

Neutral (grounded) conductors and equipment grounding conductors are bonded together at the service disconnect (and at the source or first disconnect of a separately derived system such as a transformer); in a subpanel fed from the service they must be kept on separate, isolated bars.
facts.reviewed: Said 'only at the service disconnect', which leaves out separately derived systems (transformers, generators), where bonding is also required

facts.fact: Maximum horizontal pipe support spacing includes: PVC and ABS 4 ft; CPVC 1 in and smaller 3 ft; PEX 1 in and smaller 32 in; copper tubing 1-1/4 in and smaller 6 ft; cast iron 5 ft (10 ft with 10 ft lengths); steel 12 ft.
facts.note: Card says PVC needs the most horizontal support. PVC (4 ft) needs closer support than metal pipe, but PEX and polybutylene (32 in) and small CPVC (3 ft) need even closer support.

facts.fact: Rebar can be a grounding electrode: at least 20 ft of 1/2 in or larger bar in a footing in contact with earth, encased in at least 2 in of concrete (a concrete-encased or Ufer electrode). Metal underground gas piping and aluminum may not be used as grounding electrodes.
facts.note: Card says rebar cannot be used for grounding. The NEC expressly permits concrete-encased rebar electrodes; gas piping and aluminum are the prohibited ones.

facts.fact: Underground cables under a building normally must be in a raceway, but Type MC cable listed for direct burial (and MI cable embedded in concrete or fill) may run under a building without a raceway.
facts.note: Exception added in the 2017 NEC; whether it applies depends on the NEC edition the jurisdiction has adopted.

facts.fact: For construction more than 8 ft tall, pedestrian protection depends on setback from the lot line: under 5 ft needs a barrier and covered walkway, 5 ft up to 1/4 the height needs a barrier and covered walkway, 1/4 to 1/2 the height needs a barrier, and more than 1/2 the height needs none. A 48 ft building set back 20 ft (between 12 and 24 ft) needs a barrier.
A door in the means of egress, when fully open, may not reduce the required egress width by more than 7 in, and at any position it may not reduce the required width by more than half.

Retaining walls no more than 4 ft high, measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, are exempt from a permit unless they support a surcharge or impound Class I, II or IIIA liquids.
Pedestrians must be protected by directional barricades where a walkway in front of a construction site extends into the street; such walkways must be at least 4 ft wide.
Floor members are limited to a live-load deflection of L/360 (span divided by 360); the IBC limit for total dead plus live load on floors is L/240.

Type I handrails with a circular cross section must be 1-1/4 to 2 in in outside diameter; non-circular Type I handrails must have a perimeter of 4 to 6-1/4 in and a cross section no larger than 2-1/4 in.

Fire separation distance is measured at right angles from the building face to the closest interior lot line, to the centerline of a street, alley or public way, or to an imaginary line between two buildings on the same lot.

Landings at doors must be at least as wide as the stairway or door, whichever is greater, and at least 44 in long in the direction of travel; in Group R-3, Group U and inside dwelling units the minimum length is 36 in.
Stair risers must be vertical or sloped under the tread above at no more than 30 degrees from vertical, measured from the underside of the nosing above.
Means of egress illumination must be at least 1 footcandle (11 lux) at the walking surface whenever the building is occupied.
Where floors require dampproofing, a vapor retarder such as 6-mil polyethylene is placed between the slab and base course with joints lapped at least 6 in.
Means of egress must have a ceiling height of at least 7 ft 6 in, with exceptions such as stair headroom (80 in) and limited projections and door heights.

Presumptive load-bearing values are 12,000 psf for crystalline bedrock, 4,000 psf for sedimentary and foliated rock, 3,000 psf for sandy gravel or gravel, 2,000 psf for sand and silty or clayey sands and gravels, and 1,500 psf for clays and silts.
Floors that must be waterproofed get a membrane of rubberized asphalt, butyl rubber, approved bonded HDPE or polyolefin composite, or PVC at least 6 mil thick, with joints lapped at least 6 in.
The person causing an excavation must give owners of adjoining buildings written notice at least 10 days before the scheduled start so they can protect their buildings.

Shaft enclosures (such as elevator hoistways) connecting four or more stories need at least a 2-hour fire-resistance rating; those connecting fewer than four stories need 1 hour, and never less than the floor assembly penetrated.
No cross connection, actual or potential, is allowed between a potable water system and any nonpotable system unless protected by an approved backflow prevention method.

Exposed wiring where physical damage is expected should be run in a raceway rated for it, such as rigid metal conduit, IMC, or Schedule 80 PVC; armored cable (Type AC, often called BX) is not permitted where subject to physical damage.
facts.note: Card says BX (armored cable). NEC 320.12 prohibits Type AC cable where subject to physical damage; rigid/IMC conduit or Schedule 80 PVC is the correct choice (EMT is excluded only where damage is severe).

facts.fact: In Types I and II construction, wood finish flooring may be attached to embedded or fireblocked wood sleepers, cemented to fire-resistance-rated construction, or attached to a wood subfloor on sleepers. Combustible insulating board beneath it is limited to 1/2 in thick, so 5/8-in board is not allowed.
A single hoistway enclosure may hold no more than four elevator cars, and where four or more cars serve the same part of a building they must be in at least two separate hoistways.
Stairways need at least 80 in (6 ft 8 in) of headroom, measured vertically from the line connecting the tread nosings; spiral stairs may have 78 in.
Footings must extend at least 12 in below undisturbed ground surface and also below the frost line unless they are frost-protected.
Where an elevator is required to have standby power and only one elevator is installed, it must transfer automatically to standby power within 60 seconds after normal power fails.

Soil is classified as expansive when it meets all four criteria: plasticity index of 15 or more, more than 10% passing a No. 200 sieve, more than 10% of particles smaller than 5 micrometers, and an expansion index above 20. Testing the expansion index alone is allowed in place of the first three tests.

Swinging doors serving a Group H occupancy must have panic or fire exit hardware whatever the occupant load. In Group A and E occupancies the requirement applies to rooms or spaces with an occupant load of 50 or more.
facts.note: Card says Group H doors need panic hardware at an occupant load of 50 or more. The 50-person threshold applies to Groups A and E; Group H requires panic or fire exit hardware with no occupant-load threshold.

facts.fact: A parapet is the part of a wall that extends above the roof deck; IBC 705.11 requires parapets on many exterior walls, generally at least 30 in high.
Framing for a fixed-glass curtain wall must be rigid enough to carry lateral wind loads on the glass without excessive deflection.

facts.source: Standard practice; IRC 2021 R609.4 / R703.4 (install per manufacturer)
facts.fact: Rough-opening sizes and installation details for a manufactured window such as an aluminum-clad wood unit come from the manufacturer's published data and installation instructions, which the code also requires to be followed.
A hopper window is hinged at the bottom and its top tilts inward into the room; the opposite type, hinged at the top with the bottom swinging outward, is an awning window.
A window should sit loosely in its rough opening, which is made slightly larger than the unit, so it can be shimmed plumb, level and square without being forced or racked.
In Types I and II construction, skylight frames must be noncombustible, and skylights sloped less than 45 degrees from horizontal must sit on a curb at least 4 in above the roof plane.
facts.note: Noncombustible frame rule in Types I and II is solid. The 4 in curb trigger may read 'roof pitch flatter than 3:12 unless the manufacturer specifies otherwise' in the 2021 IBC rather than 45 degrees; confirm against the code text.
facts.reviewed: Recent IBC editions may give the curb trigger as roof pitch under 3:12 rather than 45 degrees; 2021 text not confirmed

facts.fact: For resilient channels on a stud wall, the bottom channel is placed about 2 in above the floor and the top channel within 6 in of the ceiling.
facts.note: Manufacturer handbook guidance (USG); not a code requirement and may vary by edition or product.

facts.fact: When old plaster and lath are removed for a conventional plaster job, 3/8 in gypsum lath (Rocklath) is the recommended plaster base.
facts.note: Product-specific manufacturer recommendation; cannot confirm against a code.

facts.fact: A door frame that extends to the ceiling can act as a vertical control joint in a gypsum board partition.
facts.note: Manufacturer handbook guidance; not a code rule.

facts.fact: Veneer plaster drying (setting) time depends mainly on air temperature, relative humidity and air movement across the surface.
Conditions around 80 degrees F and 65% relative humidity fall within the normal drying range for veneer plaster finishes.
facts.note: Manufacturer handbook drying chart; values cannot be independently confirmed.

facts.fact: Conventional-weight all-purpose joint compound is sanded with fine paper, roughly 120 grit or finer, to avoid scuffing the board face.
facts.note: Manufacturer recommendations on grit differ by product (some say 150 or finer); cannot confirm the exact grit.

facts.fact: EIFS base-coat mesh is reinforced at critical points: doubled near inside and outside corners, diagonal mesh patches (about 9 x 12 in) at the corners of doors, windows and other openings, and mesh wrapped onto opening returns so it extends a few inches past the corner.
facts.note: Exact dimensions (8 in, 9 x 12 in, 2-1/2 in) come from manufacturer instructions and ASTM E2511/E2568 guidance, not the IBC; verify against the specific system.

facts.fact: Mechanical fasteners attaching EIFS insulation board to steel framing must penetrate the steel a minimum distance set by the system manufacturer (often cited as 5/16 in or at least three threads).
facts.note: Manufacturer-specific requirement; could not confirm a single code value.

facts.fact: Face-frame wall and base cabinets are fastened to the wall by driving screws through the horizontal hanging (hang) rails at the back of the cabinet box into the wall studs.

facts.source: NWFA installation guidelines (wood flooring over wood subfloor)
facts.fact: Before nailing solid hardwood strip flooring such as oak over a clean wood subfloor, a common recommended step is to lay 15-lb asphalt-saturated felt (or an equivalent vapor retarder) with its seams overlapped.

Wood flooring should be installed only after the building's HVAC is running and the space is held at normal living temperature and humidity, typically around 60-80 degrees F, so the wood is acclimated to in-service conditions.
facts.note: Card says 70 degrees F. Industry guidance gives a range of normal living conditions (temperature plus relative humidity) rather than a single temperature; exact ranges vary by guideline and manufacturer.

facts.fact: Medium-density fiberboard (MDF) has a dense, uniform, grain-free face, which makes it a good choice where a smooth painted finish is needed, such as cabinet panels, trim and shelving.
For gypsum-based plasters such as vermiculite plaster, the space is commonly held at 55 degrees F or above for about a week before, during, and after application until the plaster sets and dries.
facts.note: Card says 55 degrees F for a week before, during and after. This matches some manufacturer handbook guidance, but ASTM and other sources use different minimums (e.g., 40 degrees F); handbook-dependent.

facts.fact: EIFS insulation boards are set tightly together; gaps wider than about 1/16 in are filled with slivers of insulation, not base coat, and board joints are staggered and offset from sheathing joints and from the corners of openings.
facts.note: Cards say 1/16 in maximum gap and 6 in offset from sheathing joints and opening corners. These come from manufacturer instructions; offset distances differ by manufacturer (6-8 in).

facts.source: EIFS evaluation reports (ICC-ES AC219) / manufacturer specs
facts.fact: EIFS foam insulation board has a minimum thickness (commonly 3/4 in) and a maximum set by the system's evaluation report (commonly about 4 in).
facts.note: Card says maximum thickness 3/4 in; 3/4 in is usually cited as the MINIMUM. Limits are product-specific, so I did not mark this corrected.

facts.fact: EIFS reinforcing mesh must run continuously around corners and overlap adjoining mesh, including back-wrapped mesh, by a minimum commonly specified as 2-1/2 in.
facts.note: Cards 430 and 469 say 2-1/2 in. This is a manufacturer-handbook requirement, not a model-code provision.

facts.source: EPA indoor air quality guidance on volatile organic compounds
facts.fact: To limit worker and occupant exposure to volatile organic compounds (VOCs), choose low-VOC or low-emitting products. Store VOC-containing materials sealed, in a well-ventilated area kept apart from occupied spaces.
Wet-spray cellulose insulation must dry to a low moisture content (often cited as below about 19%) before drywall is installed over it.
facts.note: Manufacturer limits vary (some allow up to 25%); the 19% figure cannot be confirmed as a single standard.

facts.fact: The best way to limit VOC exposure is to choose low-VOC (low-emitting) products and to store VOC-containing materials in a well-ventilated area sealed off from occupied spaces.
In cooling mode, a properly charged and airflow-balanced air conditioner typically shows a temperature drop (evaporator delta-T) of roughly 16 to 22 degrees F between return air and supply air.
facts.note: Industry rule of thumb, not a code requirement; target delta-T varies with humidity, airflow and equipment (many sources cite 15-20 degrees F).

facts.fact: Blown-in loose-fill insulation (cellulose or fiberglass) is the usual method for adding insulation to existing homes, since it can be blown into attics and dense-packed into closed wall cavities without removing finishes.
Unfaced batt insulation is friction-fit between studs and needs no stapling; faced batts are stapled through their flanges.
New construction generates roughly 4 lb of waste per square foot of building area.
facts.note: Commonly cited estimate (NAHB studies show roughly 4.0 to 4.4 lb/sq ft for new homes); varies by building type and source.

facts.source: State erosion and sediment control manuals
facts.fact: Where gravel is used to backfill a silt fence trench, washed stone of about 3/4 in to 1-1/2 in is typical.
facts.note: Silt fence details vary by state BMP manual and project specification; could not confirm a national standard.

facts.fact: LEED-certified buildings are often reported to use about 25 to 30 percent less energy on average than comparable conventional buildings.
facts.note: Widely quoted figure from early studies; actual savings vary widely by building and certification level.

facts.fact: Silt fences are installed along the contour at the toe (bottom) of disturbed slopes, downslope of the work, to trap sediment carried by sheet flow.
LEED is a voluntary, third-party green building certification program run by the U.S. Green Building Council that gives a common standard for measuring high-performance, sustainable buildings.

LEED credit categories include Sustainable Sites, Water Efficiency, Energy and Atmosphere, Materials and Resources, Indoor Environmental Quality, Innovation and Regional Priority (LEED v4 adds Location and Transportation and Integrative Process).
Polyisocyanurate insulation boards are commonly made in 4 ft (48 in) widths and lengths up to about 10 ft (120 in).
facts.note: Product sizes are set by manufacturers and vary; not a code requirement.

facts.source: State erosion and sediment control manuals
facts.fact: Silt fence posts are typically spaced no more than about 6 ft apart and driven at least 12 in into the ground.
facts.note: Post spacing (often 6 to 10 ft) and embedment (12 to 18 in) vary by state BMP manual and fabric backing.

facts.fact: Before insulating an attic or ceiling, check recessed light fixtures: unless a fixture is rated Type IC for insulation contact, insulation must be kept at least 3 in from it and not placed over it.
The kraft paper facing on batt insulation serves as a vapor retarder (a Class II vapor retarder under the IRC) and is installed toward the warm-in-winter side of the wall.

facts.source: USG Gypsum Construction Handbook (joint compound coverage)
facts.fact: About 9.4 gallons of ready-mixed lightweight all-purpose joint compound are estimated to finish 1,000 sq ft of gypsum board.
facts.note: Product-specific coverage figure from a manufacturer handbook; varies by product and finish level.

facts.fact: For a straight partition, studs = (length in inches / spacing) + 1; a 12 ft wall at 16 in on center needs 144/16 + 1 = 10 studs before adding for corners, openings or waste.
When excavated, blasted rock swells the most (roughly 50-65% from bank to loose volume), more than clay, loam or sand, so it needs the most haul capacity per bank cubic yard.
Trench volume = average width x depth x length. A trench 18 ft wide at the top, 5 ft wide at the bottom, 8 ft deep and 750 ft long holds (18+5)/2 x 8 x 750 = 69,000 cu ft (about 2,556 cu yd).
facts.note: Card states an 18-inch top width but answers 69,000 cu ft, which only works with an 18-ft top width; with 18 in the volume would be 19,500 cu ft.

facts.fact: Loam shrinks when compacted relative to its bank volume; one textbook shrinkage factor given for loam is about 0.83.
facts.note: Shrinkage and load factors vary by reference table (common values for loam range about 0.80-0.90); cannot confirm 0.83 as standard.

facts.fact: A rough estimate of wood truss weight is about 15 lb per linear foot, so a bundle of seven 32 ft trusses weighs roughly 7 x 32 x 15 = 3,360 lb.
facts.note: Rule-of-thumb figure; actual truss weight varies widely with depth, lumber and design.

facts.fact: Life-cycle costing compares alternatives using initial, operating, maintenance and replacement costs plus future benefits over the useful life of a building or system, not first cost alone.
Loose volume is converted to bank volume by dividing by (1 + swell), so 700 loose cubic yards per hour of soil with 35 percent swell equals about 519 bank cubic yards per hour.

facts.source: Equipment productivity rule of thumb (Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods)
facts.fact: A naturally aspirated (non-turbocharged) engine loses roughly 3% of its rated power for every 1,000 ft of elevation above sea level, which reduces equipment output on high-altitude jobs.
Excavated soil swells in volume: typical published swell from bank to loose condition is about 10-15% for sand and gravel, about 20-25% for loam or common earth, and about 25-40% for clay.
facts.note: Cards say loam 20% and excavated clay 25%. Swell percentages vary by table and material condition; values are approximate and not code-based.

facts.source: RSMeans square foot / assemblies cost data (area modifier method)
facts.fact: RSMeans square-foot costs are adjusted for building size by comparing the proposed area to the typical size for that building type; a project larger than typical gets a cost multiplier below 1.0 and a smaller one gets a multiplier above 1.0.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: labor estimating
facts.fact: Labor cost for a task is based on quantity, crew make-up and wage rates, and productivity (output per hour) under the job conditions; the logic links between activities affect the schedule, not the labor cost of the task.
Board feet equal thickness (in) times width (in) times length (ft), divided by 12; a 2 in by 10 in board 9 ft long contains 15 board feet.
Excavation is estimated by the volume of earth removed in cubic yards, found by dividing cubic feet by 27.
An enclosed fire service access elevator lobby must be at least 150 sq ft with no dimension less than 8 ft.
Spray-applied fireproofing on steel generally requires ambient and substrate temperatures of at least 40 degrees F during application and for about 24 hours after.
facts.note: Temperature limits come from product manufacturers, not the IBC; values vary by product.

facts.fact: Where fire-protective covering on a structural member could be damaged by vehicles, material handling or similar activity, it must be protected by corner guards or a metal or noncombustible jacket at least 5 ft above the finished floor.

Fire protection systems must pass acceptance tests, conducted in the presence of the fire code official when required, and it is unlawful to occupy any portion of a structure until the required detection, alarm and suppression systems have been tested and approved.
facts.reviewed: IFC 901.5 requires the tests to be witnessed by the fire code official only when required; the occupancy prohibition is in 901.5.1

facts.fact: Buildings with fire service access elevators must be fully sprinklered, except that sprinklers may not be installed in the machine rooms, machinery spaces, control rooms, control spaces or hoistways of those elevators.

Extinguisher cabinets generally may not be locked, but in Group I-3 occupancies and mental health areas of Group I-2 occupancies, extinguishers may be locked up or kept at staff locations if staff have keys.

Any story or basement over 1,500 sq ft must be sprinklered unless it has qualifying exterior openings for fire department access, and each such opening must have a minimum dimension of at least 30 in.

In high-rise buildings 420 ft or less in height, fire barriers around vertical shafts (other than interior exit stairways and elevator hoistways) may be reduced to a 1-hour rating if automatic sprinklers are installed in the shafts at the top and at alternate floors.
A clearance of at least 3 ft is required between automatic sprinklers and the top of piles of loose combustible fibers.
facts.note: Could not confirm the exact IFC section or value; general storage uses an 18 in clearance below sprinkler deflectors.

facts.fact: When a fire-rated column extends through a ceiling, its fire protection must run continuously from the top of the foundation or floor/ceiling assembly below, through the ceiling space, to the top of the column.
Manual fire alarm boxes (pull stations) must be within 5 ft of the entrance to each exit, with the operable part 42 to 48 in above the floor.

Once construction is more than 40 ft above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access, a temporary or permanent stairway is required, extended as work progresses to within one floor of the highest point with secured decking or flooring.

In NFPA 13 systems, sprinklers are not required in clothes closets, linen closets and pantries inside hotel or motel guest units when the space is 24 sq ft or less and its walls and ceiling are surfaced with noncombustible or limited-combustible materials.

The manual pull station for a commercial kitchen hood suppression system must be at or near an egress path from the cooking area, 10 to 20 ft from the kitchen exhaust system, and mounted 42 to 48 in above the floor.

In a high-rise, fuel lines supplying a generator inside the building must be separated from other areas (other than the generator room) by an approved method or assembly rated at least 2 hours; where the building is fully sprinklered, the rating may be reduced to 1 hour.
facts.reviewed: Leaves out the reduction to 1 hour in a fully sprinklered building, which covers nearly every high-rise

facts.fact: Required emergency and standby power systems must supply their loads for at least 2 hours without refueling or recharging unless another section of the code states a different duration.

In Type V buildings with NFPA 13R systems, exterior balconies and decks with a roof or deck above must be sprinklered; sidewall heads may have deflectors 1 to 6 in below the structural members and no more than 14 in below the underside of an open-wood-joist deck.
Automatic sprinklers are needed beneath covered kiosks, display booths, concession stands and similar obstructions that exceed 4 ft in width, because the cover blocks overhead sprinkler discharge.
facts.note: Consistent with the NFPA 13 rule for obstructions wider than 4 ft, but could not pin the exact IFC/IBC section the card relies on.

facts.fact: In new Group R buildings, smoke alarms must get their primary power from the building wiring, with battery backup, and with no disconnecting switch other than the overcurrent protection.

Hand-held portable fire extinguishers must be mounted with at least 4 in of clearance between the floor and the bottom of the extinguisher; the top may be no higher than 5 ft for units of 40 lb or less, or 3-1/2 ft for heavier units.
Doors in fire-resistance-rated corridor walls need a fire protection rating of at least 20 minutes (1/3 hour) and must also meet smoke and draft control requirements.

Transom assemblies above doors in fire-resistance-rated walls must meet the rating requirements in IBC Section 716, which for some 2-hour assemblies call for fire-resistance-rated (not just fire-protection-rated) glazing.
facts.note: Card says a transom in a 2-hour exterior wall needs a 2-hour rating. Table 716.1(2) gives 1-1/2 hr for doors in 2-hr exterior walls, and transom rules depend on wall type and glazing; could not confirm the card's figure.

facts.fact: Smoke barriers generally need a 1-hour fire-resistance rating, but in Group I-3 (detention) buildings they may be built of steel sheet at least 0.10 in thick.
Valves controlling the water supply to automatic sprinkler systems, along with waterflow switches and other critical components, must be electrically supervised by a listed fire alarm control unit.

Shaft enclosures such as elevator hoistways must be rated 2 hours when they connect four or more stories and 1 hour when they connect fewer than four, and never less than the floor assembly they pass through.

Where walls or ceilings required to be fire-resistance-rated or noncombustible have interior finish set out on furring strips, the concealed spaces between furring must be filled with Class A material or fireblocked at intervals of no more than 8 ft in any direction.
facts.note: Card says 8 inches. The IBC fireblocking interval for furred interior finish is 8 FEET in every direction.
facts.reviewed: The code says the spaces are filled with Class A material, not noncombustible material. The rule also applies only where the wall or ceiling must be rated or noncombustible.

facts.fact: A fire extinguisher rated at least 2A is required for each 3,000 sq ft of protected building area, with travel distance to one no more than 100 ft; one 55-gallon open drum of water with two fire pails may substitute for a 2A extinguisher, and an extinguisher rated at least 10B must be within 50 ft wherever more than 5 gallons of flammable liquid or 5 lb of flammable gas is used.

Soda-acid and other water-based extinguishers are rated only for Class A fires (ordinary combustibles); Class B fires involving flammable liquids, gasoline, oil, paint or grease need carbon dioxide, dry chemical or foam extinguishers.
No more than 25 gallons of flammable liquids may be stored in a room outside an approved storage cabinet; larger quantities belong in approved cabinets or storage rooms.
A single flammable liquid storage cabinet may hold no more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2 or 3 flammable liquids, or no more than 120 gallons of Category 4 flammable liquids.
Solvent waste, oily rags and flammable liquids must be kept in fire-resistant covered containers until they are removed from the worksite.

Fireblocking slows the spread of flame and gases through concealed spaces; in wood stud walls it is required vertically at ceiling and floor levels and horizontally at intervals of no more than 10 ft.
Repointing (tuckpointing) mortar should be prehydrated before use and is usually a Type N or softer mortar so it is not stronger than the original masonry.
Grout mixed with more water than specified can segregate (aggregate separates from the paste) and shrink excessively in the cells.
Abrasive blasting of brick is done at low to moderate nozzle pressure, roughly 60-100 psi, to avoid damaging the brick face and mortar joints.
facts.note: Card gives 60-100 'psf', an obvious unit error for psi. Recommended pressures vary by source and abrasive; cannot confirm the exact range.

facts.source: TMS 402 composite wall ties (referenced by IBC 2021 Ch. 21)
facts.fact: In composite masonry walls, wire wall ties may be spaced no more than 36 in apart horizontally and 24 in apart vertically.

Anchored masonry (brick) veneer must be supported on concrete or masonry footings or foundations or other approved noncombustible support; the IRC allows limited exceptions such as steel angles over openings and support on wood framing under specific weight and height conditions.
In a masonry fireplace, the smoke shelf behind the damper turns back cold downdrafts coming down the flue so they do not push smoke into the room.

Common (American) bond is running bond with a course of full-length headers placed periodically, typically every sixth course (every fifth to seventh), to tie wythes together structurally and create the pattern.
In stack bond all head (vertical) joints line up, so units do not overlap and horizontal joint reinforcement is normally needed for strength.
Tooled concave and V-shaped mortar joints are the most weather-resistant and are recommended where walls face heavy rain and high winds, because tooling compresses the mortar and sheds water.
The excavated base for brick paving is graded to roughly the same slope as the finished surface, on the order of 1/8 to 1/4 in per foot, so water drains.
facts.note: Brick paving slope recommendations vary by source and use (pedestrian vs vehicular); could not confirm the card's exact range.

facts.fact: A head joint is the vertical mortar joint between masonry units and a bed joint is the horizontal one; a stack bond aligns units directly above one another so the vertical joints are continuous.

Mortar should be used within about 2-1/2 hours of mixing in warm weather (80 degrees F or above); mortar may be retempered with water only to replace evaporation, and mortar that has stiffened from hydration (begun to set) must be discarded.

Parging is applying a thin coat of mortar or cement plaster over masonry such as block foundation walls, and a lintel is a beam over an opening that carries loads around it, like a header in a wood wall.
On a topographic map, contour lines that close on themselves mark a hilltop (summit) or a depression; depression contours are often drawn with hachure tick marks pointing downhill.
Contour lines spaced closely together indicate steep ground, and widely spaced contours indicate gentle slopes.
A concave slope (steep at the top, flattening toward the bottom) shows contour lines bunched near the top and spreading apart toward the base; a convex slope shows the opposite.
The 3-4-5 method (or any multiple such as 6-8-10) uses a right triangle to check that building corners are square during layout.
A contour line connects points of equal elevation above or below a reference datum.
Residential floor plans are commonly drawn at 1/4 in = 1 ft-0 in, and dimension lines show the distance between the two points they connect.

A foundation plan is a top (plan) view of footings and foundation walls, an elevation is a side view showing height and width, and a detail is an enlarged drawing of a small or complex part of the building.

A schedule is a table or chart on the drawings (doors, windows, finishes, fixtures), and specifications are the written requirements for materials, workmanship and methods that accompany the drawings.

When a follow-on activity can begin a set number of days after a predecessor begins (for example, painting starting 7 days after drywall starts), the link is a start-to-start relationship with a lag of that many days.

When a subcontractor reports a conflict in the specifications, the project manager should evaluate its cost and schedule impact and send a request for information (RFI) to the design professional for a resolution rather than deciding it alone.
Job site space allocation is the part of the site layout plan that designates areas for material delivery and storage, temporary offices, sanitary facilities, parking and equipment.

As-built (record) drawings document final dimensions, locations of concealed utilities and facilities, and all changes from the contract drawings, and they should be kept in a secure, retrievable location for the owner's future use.

As-built drawings are most accurate when marked up continuously in the field by the superintendent or foreman who sees the work installed; the office-based project manager is the least likely to produce accurate as-builts.
Receiving and storing materials as close as practical to where they will be installed cuts double handling, lowers cost and improves worker productivity.

Shop drawings are needed for custom-fabricated items such as structural steel, millwork, curtain wall and ductwork; standard off-the-shelf products like sheet vinyl flooring are usually submitted as product data and samples instead.
When the general contractor rejects a subcontractor's shop drawings, they are returned to the subcontractor to be revised and resubmitted before being forwarded to the architect.
Building Information Modeling (BIM) is a shared digital model of a project that is continually updated and can link cost (5D) and schedule (4D) data to improve coordination, productivity and quality.

Shop drawings are prepared by the fabricator or subcontractor to show exactly how an item will be fabricated and installed, letting the design team confirm it meets design intent before production begins.
Project closeout includes turning over spare parts and attic stock, O&M manuals, warranties, as-built drawings, keys and final lien releases, along with punch list completion and owner training.
On a small or tight site, the delivery point must account for traffic patterns, enough room for delivery trucks to stand and maneuver, and access for unloading equipment such as forklifts or cranes.
The American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) publishes the main industry standards for commissioning and for testing, adjusting and balancing HVAC systems.
Value engineering seeks the required function and quality at the lowest life-cycle cost. It can happen at any stage, but the most savings come early in design, when changes are cheapest to make.

Submittals (shop drawings, product data sheets, and samples) are sent by the contractor to the designer to confirm that the proposed materials and products meet the contract documents; product data sheets show manufacturer specifications.

FAA Form 7460-1 notice must be filed at least 45 days before construction when a structure or crane would exceed FAA notice criteria, such as being more than 200 ft above ground or penetrating a 100:1 imaginary surface extending 20,000 ft from a public-use airport runway longer than 3,200 ft.
facts.note: Card says to contact the airport 30 days before using a crane within 5 miles of an airport. The governing rule is FAA 14 CFR Part 77, which requires notice to the FAA (Form 7460-1) at least 45 days in advance when notice criteria are met; distance is measured from the runway, not a flat 5 miles.

facts.fact: Enclosed attics and enclosed rafter spaces need a total net free ventilating area of at least 1/150 of the area of the vented space. It may be reduced to 1/300 only when 40-50% of the required vent area is in the upper part of the attic (no more than 3 ft below the ridge) and, in Climate Zones 6-8, a Class I or II vapor retarder is installed on the warm-in-winter side of the ceiling.
Passive attic ventilation uses natural airflow: air enters through soffit or eave vents and exits through ridge vents, with no fans.

Sillcocks, hose bibbs, wall hydrants and other hose connections must have backflow protection from an atmospheric-type or pressure-type vacuum breaker or a permanently attached hose-connection vacuum breaker.
A kitchen sink needs a 1-1/2 in trap, including when it serves a food waste disposer and dishwasher.
A masonry chimney must extend at least 3 ft above the highest point where it passes through the roof and at least 2 ft higher than any part of the building within 10 ft.

Exterior wood siding, sheathing and wall framing less than 6 in above the ground, or less than 2 in above concrete steps, porches, patios or similar exposed surfaces, must be naturally durable or preservative-treated wood.

Interior masonry chimneys (including where they pass through floors and roofs) need at least 2 in of air space clearance to combustibles; chimneys located entirely outside the exterior walls need at least 1 in.

In dwellings, receptacles installed within 6 ft of the top inside edge of a sink bowl must have GFCI protection; the IRC states this for 125-volt, 15- and 20-amp receptacles, and NEC 2020 extends dwelling GFCI rules to all 125- through 250-volt receptacles on circuits of 150 V or less to ground.
facts.reviewed: Wording is from NEC 2017; NEC 2020 210.8(A) covers 125 V through 250 V receptacles in dwellings

facts.fact: A floor drain must have a waste outlet of at least 2 in diameter and a removable strainer, and it must be built so the drain can be cleaned.

An atmospheric (Category I) gas water heater is typically vented with listed Type B double-wall gas vent, sized from the IFGC vent tables and the manufacturer's instructions based on appliance input and vent height; there is no single required diameter.
facts.note: Card says a water heater needs a 4 in double-wall Type B vent. Type B is correct for Category I appliances, but the diameter is sized per the vent tables and listing (3 in and 4 in are both common); power-vent and condensing units use other venting.

facts.fact: When threading 1/2 in steel gas pipe, about 10 threads are cut, for a threaded length of roughly 3/4 in.

A 240-volt-only single-phase load needs two ungrounded (hot) circuit conductors plus an equipment grounding conductor; a 120/240-volt load adds a grounded (neutral) conductor, for three circuit conductors plus the ground.
facts.note: Card says 4 leads are used as circuit conductors. The equipment grounding conductor is not a circuit conductor, so a 240 V load uses 2 circuit conductors and a 120/240 V load uses 3.

facts.fact: Black (uncoated) steel pipe is the standard material for natural gas piping, and gas piping concealed in walls may not contain unions, tubing fittings, bushings, compression couplings, right-and-left couplings or swing joints.

Where eave or soffit vents are installed, attic insulation must not block airflow, and at least 1 in of space must be kept between the insulation and the roof sheathing at the vent location (baffles are typically used).

Drip edge at eaves and gables must overlap adjacent pieces by at least 2 in, extend at least 1/4 in below the roof sheathing, and extend at least 2 in back onto the roof deck; at the eave it goes under the underlayment.
The bottom of the clear opening of an emergency escape and rescue opening may be no more than 44 in above the floor.
facts.reviewed: 2021 IRC renumbered R310.2 subsections; cite the parent section

facts.fact: Impervious surfaces such as paving within 10 ft of a building foundation must slope at least 2 percent away from the building; landscaped grade must fall at least 6 in within the first 10 ft.
Gravel or crushed-stone foundation drains must extend at least 1 ft beyond the outside edge of the footing and 6 in above its top, and be covered with an approved filter membrane.
Smoke alarms must be placed at least 3 ft horizontally from the door or opening of a bathroom that contains a tub or shower, unless that would prevent a required placement.

In sawn-lumber floor joists, notches may not be placed in the middle one-third of the span; notches in the top or bottom edge elsewhere are limited to 1/6 of the joist depth and a length of 1/3 of the depth, and notches at the ends (bearing) are limited to 1/4 of the depth.

Where perforated pipe or drain tile is used for a foundation drain, its invert may not be higher than the floor, it is placed on at least 2 in of gravel or crushed stone and covered with at least 6 in, and the top of the joints or perforations is protected with a filter membrane; laying perforations facing down is common practice.
facts.reviewed: Mixes up the gravel-drain dimensions with the pipe-drain rule, and presents holes-down as a code requirement

facts.fact: Collar ties connecting opposing rafters must be in the upper third of the attic space, at least 1x4 nominal, and spaced no more than 4 ft on center, which is every third rafter pair when rafters are 16 in on center.
facts.note: Card says every fourth pair of rafters at 16 in o.c. That is 64 in apart; the IRC limits collar tie spacing to 4 ft o.c., i.e., every third pair at 16 in o.c.

facts.fact: Both standard EIFS and EIFS with drainage must stop at least 6 in above the finished ground level.

Roof purlins are supported by 2x4 (minimum) struts running to bearing walls at a slope of at least 45 degrees from horizontal; struts may be at most 4 ft on center with an unbraced length of no more than 8 ft.
facts.note: Card says purlin struts shall not exceed 8 inches in length. The IRC limit is 8 FEET of unbraced strut length (with slope not less than 45 degrees).

facts.fact: Sill plates are anchored with at least 1/2-in bolts embedded at least 7 in into the concrete or grouted masonry, spaced no more than 6 ft apart, with a bolt within 12 in of each plate end and at least two per plate section.

In crawl spaces, wood joists or the underside of a wood structural floor closer than 18 in to exposed ground, and wood girders closer than 12 in, must be naturally durable or preservative-treated wood.
facts.note: Card says 13 in. The IRC thresholds are 18 in for floor joists and 12 in for girders above exposed ground in under-floor spaces.

facts.fact: Foundation walls that retain earth and enclose interior space or floors below grade must be dampproofed on the exterior from the top of the footing to finished grade; waterproofing is required instead where a high water table or severe soil-water conditions exist.

Notches in solid lumber floor joists may not exceed 1/6 of the joist depth, be longer than 1/3 of the depth, or be located in the middle third of the span; end notches may not exceed 1/4 of the depth, and bored holes may not exceed 1/3 of the depth or be within 2 in of the top or bottom edge.
Ends of ceiling joists (and floor joists) must have at least 1-1/2 in of bearing on wood or metal and at least 3 in of bearing on masonry or concrete.
Each wood shingle or wood shake must be attached with two fasteners, which must be corrosion resistant.

Drip edge on shingle roofs must be mechanically fastened at no more than 12 in on center, overlap adjacent pieces at least 2 in, extend at least 1/4 in below the sheathing, and extend at least 2 in back onto the deck.
On shingle roofs, drip edge goes under the underlayment at eaves and over the underlayment along rake edges.

Asphalt shingles must be attached with corrosion-resistant roofing nails (galvanized steel, stainless steel, aluminum or copper) with at least a 12-gauge shank and a 3/8 in head; staples are not an approved fastener.
Gutters are commonly pitched about 1/16 in per foot toward the downspout, which gives roughly 1-3/8 in of fall over a 22-ft gutter run.
facts.note: Gutter pitch is a manufacturer/trade recommendation, not a model-code requirement; published guidance ranges from about 1/4 in per 10 ft up to 1/4 in per ft.

facts.fact: Field seams between EPDM membrane sheets are made with primed seam (splice) tape or splice adhesive, and the exposed seam edges are finished with lap sealant (caulk).

The aggregate (gravel) surfacing on a built-up roof embedded in the flood coat shields the bitumen and felts from UV, heat, drying and weathering, and also adds fire resistance and protection from foot traffic and hail.

Valley flashing for wood shingle and wood shake roofs must be corrosion-resistant sheet metal of at least No. 26 gage; open, metal-lined valleys are the standard installation practice for these roofs.
facts.reviewed: The code sets the valley flashing material and gage but does not ban woven or closed-cut valleys

facts.source: IRC 2021 R905.7 / R905.8 (wood shingles and shakes)
facts.fact: Spaced (skip) sheathing, where boards are laid with gaps between them so the roofing can breathe and dry, is a permitted deck for wood shingle and wood shake roofs; most other roof coverings require solid sheathing.
Gutter runs are commonly limited so that the high point is no more than roughly 25 to 40 ft from a downspout; longer runs get a downspout at each end with the gutter pitched toward both.
facts.note: Card says 25 ft maximum from high point to downspout. This is a trade rule of thumb, not a code requirement, and published guidance varies (often 30-40 ft). Not exam-confirmed.

facts.fact: Counterflashing is fastened to or set into the wall and turned down over the top edge of the base flashing, shedding water past that edge while letting the roof and wall move independently.

On low-slope roofs (below 4:12) receiving photovoltaic or asphalt shingles, the IRC calls for a double-coverage underlayment application, with specified end laps that are staggered between courses (one cited figure is 4-in end laps offset 6 ft).
facts.note: Card says 4-in end laps offset 6 ft for slopes 3:12 to 4:12. Underlayment application tables and PV shingle slope limits changed between IRC editions; could not confirm the exact 2021 values.

facts.fact: Under the OSH Act the employer is responsible for providing a workplace free from recognized hazards (the General Duty Clause) and for complying with OSHA standards.
When an OSHA standard requires an emergency action plan, it must be written if the employer has more than 10 employees (11 or more); employers with 10 or fewer may communicate the plan orally.

Under the Hazard Communication Standard, a Safety Data Sheet (SDS, formerly MSDS) for each hazardous chemical must be kept and be readily accessible to employees during every work shift; SDSs follow a standardized 16-section format.
An oxygen-deficient atmosphere contains less than 19.5% oxygen by volume; an oxygen-enriched atmosphere contains more than 23.5%.
A temporary radiant-type room heater must have at least 36 in of clearance to combustible material at its sides.

An anchorage for personal fall arrest must support at least 5,000 lb per employee attached, or be designed, installed and used under a qualified person's supervision as part of a complete system with a safety factor of at least two.
facts.note: Card says 5,400 lb dead weight. That figure is the lifeline anchorage requirement in 29 CFR 1926.104(b); the personal fall arrest anchorage requirement in 1926.502(d)(15) is 5,000 lb per attached employee.
facts.reviewed: Note calls 1926.104 'old'; its 5,400 lb lifeline figure is still in the CFR

facts.fact: Driveways between and around outdoor combustible storage piles must be at least 15 ft wide, kept clear, and spaced so no grid unit exceeds 50 ft by 150 ft.
Outdoor piles of combustible materials must be stable and may never be stacked higher than 20 ft.
In open yard storage areas, portable fire extinguishers rated at least 2A must be placed so the travel distance to the nearest one does not exceed 100 ft.
A stairway or ladder must be provided at every point of worker access where there is a break in elevation of 19 in or more, unless a ramp, runway, embankment or personnel hoist is provided.

A competent person must inspect excavations, adjacent areas and protective systems daily before work starts and as needed during the shift, and again after every rainstorm or other event that increases the hazard.
An emergency action plan must be written, kept at the workplace and available to employees when the employer has more than 10 employees; with 10 or fewer it may be communicated orally.

The FAA must be notified at least 45 days ahead (Form 7460-1) for a crane or structure more than 200 ft above ground, or one that would penetrate a 100:1 slope within 20,000 ft (about 3.8 mi) of a public-use airport runway longer than 3,200 ft (50:1 within 10,000 ft for shorter runways, 25:1 within 5,000 ft of a heliport).
facts.note: Card says 5 miles. FAA notice under 14 CFR 77.9 is based on height and imaginary-surface slopes within 20,000 ft, 10,000 ft or 5,000 ft depending on the facility, not a 5-mile radius.

facts.fact: When a portable ladder is used to reach an upper landing, its side rails must extend at least 3 ft above the upper landing surface (or the ladder must be secured with a grab device if that is not possible).

Suspension scaffold ropes must be inspected by a competent person before each shift and replaced if there are 6 randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay or 3 broken wires in one strand in one lay, as well as for kinks, heat or electrical damage, or wear exceeding one-third of the outside wire diameter.
Grinding machines with abrasive wheels must be fitted with safety guards (protection hoods) that cover the spindle end, nut and flange projections and are strong enough to contain a bursting wheel.

A competent person must inspect excavations and their protective systems; departing from a manufacturer's tabulated data for shoring or shielding requires the manufacturer's specific written approval, and engineered designs must be approved by a registered professional engineer.
facts.note: Card says the excavator (equipment operator) may change or adjust the shoring method. OSHA places inspection with the competent person and requires manufacturer or registered PE approval for deviations from tabulated or engineered designs.

facts.fact: LP-gas containers stored outdoors awaiting use must be kept from the nearest building by distance based on quantity: 500 lb or less needs no separation, 501 to 6,000 lb needs 10 ft, 6,001 to 10,000 lb needs 20 ft, and over 10,000 lb needs 25 ft. Storing LP-gas inside buildings is prohibited.
No more than 25 gallons of flammable liquids may be stored in a room outside of an approved storage cabinet on a construction site.
facts.note: Card says 25 gallons not in an approved container. The OSHA limit applies to liquids kept outside an approved storage cabinet; approved containers are still required for the liquids themselves.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P App. A and B
facts.fact: In the OSHA Appendix B sloping table, stable rock is the only classification allowed a vertical (90 degree) slope. Other exceptions exist: excavations under 5 ft deep may skip a protective system when a competent person finds no sign of cave-in, and Type A soil allows a vertical lower portion up to 3-1/2 ft in certain configurations.
facts.reviewed: 'Only' overstates it: excavations under 5 ft (competent-person check) and the 3-1/2 ft vertical lower portion allowed in Type A also apply

facts.fact: First aid kit contents must be in a weatherproof container with individually sealed packages, and the employer must check the kit before it goes to each job and at least weekly on each job to replace used items.

Scaffolds must be kept at least 3 ft from insulated power lines under 300 volts and at least 10 ft from insulated lines of 300 V to 50 kV and from uninsulated lines under 50 kV, with greater clearance for higher voltages.
OSHA requirements for concrete formwork, shoring and reshoring are in Subpart Q, Concrete and Masonry Construction.

A roof warning line must be set at least 6 ft back from the roof edge, flagged with high-visibility material at intervals of no more than 6 ft, with its lowest point (including sag) 34 to 39 in above the walking surface.
facts.note: Card says warning lines are flagged at not more than 6 ft from the roof edge. The 6 ft is the minimum setback from the edge; the flagging interval is a separate maximum of 6 ft.

facts.fact: In excavation terms, a kickout is the accidental release or failure of a cross brace in a shoring system.

In construction, workers on a walking or working surface with an unprotected side or edge 6 ft or more above a lower level must be protected by guardrails, safety nets or personal fall arrest systems.
A portable fire extinguisher rated at least 2A is required for each 3,000 sq ft of protected building area, and travel distance from any point to the nearest extinguisher may not exceed 100 ft.
A scaffold platform generally may be no more than 14 in from the face of the work, but for plastering and lathing operations the limit is 18 in.
Outdoor piles of flammable-liquid containers (60 gal or less each) may not exceed 1,100 gal per pile, must be separated from each other by 5 ft, and may be no closer than 20 ft to a building.
Temporary radiant-type room heaters need at least 36 in of clearance to combustibles at the sides and rear (circulating-type room heaters need 12 in), and 18 in at the chimney connector.
Walkways must be provided where workers or equipment cross over excavations, and guardrails are required on walkways that are 6 ft or more above the lower level.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P App. B, Table B-1
facts.fact: For excavations under 20 ft deep, OSHA's maximum allowable slopes are 3/4H:1V (53 degrees) in Type A soil, 1H:1V (45 degrees) in Type B soil, and 1-1/2H:1V (34 degrees) in Type C soil.

OSHA presumes that thermal system insulation and sprayed or troweled surfacing materials in buildings built no later than 1980, as well as asphalt and vinyl flooring installed by then, contain asbestos unless testing proves otherwise.

During steel erection, routes for suspended loads must be pre-planned so no one works directly below a suspended load, except employees making the initial connection of the steel or employees needed to hook or unhook the load.
facts.reviewed: 1926.753(d)(1) allows only initial connection and hooking/unhooking; 'guiding' is not listed (it comes from the crane rule 1926.1425)

facts.fact: Ladder jack scaffold platforms may not exceed 20 ft in height.
facts.reviewed: Current 1926.452(k) has no 'light duty' language (that was the pre-1996 rule)

facts.fact: Portable power-driven circular saws must have guards above and below the base plate (shoe), and the lower guard must return automatically to cover the blade.

An emergency action plan must cover evacuation and escape procedures and routes, procedures for workers who stay to run critical operations, accounting for employees after evacuation, rescue and medical duties, and how to report emergencies.
Each employee on a single-point or two-point adjustable suspension scaffold must be protected by both a personal fall arrest system and a guardrail system.

Employees constructing a leading edge 6 ft or more above a lower level must be protected by guardrails, safety nets or personal fall arrest, or by a fall protection plan if those are shown to be infeasible.
Electric power tools must be either grounded or of the approved double-insulated type.
Employees at the edge of an excavation 6 ft or more deep must be protected by guardrails, fences or barricades when the excavation is hidden by plant growth or another visual barrier.
Excavated spoil, materials and equipment must be kept at least 2 ft from the edge of an excavation or held back by retaining devices.
Bagged materials must be stacked by stepping back the layers and cross-keying the bags at least every 10 bags high.
A competent person must inspect cranes each shift, including air, hydraulic and other pressurized lines for deterioration or leakage.

Materials stored inside buildings under construction may not be placed within 6 ft of hoistways or floor openings, nor within 10 ft of an exterior wall that does not extend above the top of the stored material.
A confined-space atmosphere is oxygen-enriched above 23.5 percent oxygen by volume and oxygen-deficient below 19.5 percent.

Electrical equipment operating at 0 to 150 volts to ground needs at least 3 ft of clear working space in front of it and at least 30 in wide (or the equipment width). Headroom is 6 ft 3 in under OSHA 1926.403 and 6-1/2 ft under NEC 110.26(A)(3).
facts.note: Card says 3 square feet. The requirement is a 3 ft working depth (a distance), plus 30 in width and 6.5 ft headroom, not an area.
facts.reviewed: OSHA 1926.403(i)(1)(v) requires 6 ft 3 in headroom; 6-1/2 ft is the NEC figure, so the combined citation was inconsistent

facts.fact: Trenches 4 ft or more deep must have a stairway, ladder, ramp or other safe exit placed so workers travel no more than 25 ft laterally to reach it.
Hook-on and attachable ladders on supported scaffolds over 35 ft high must have rest platforms at vertical intervals of no more than 35 ft.
facts.reviewed: The 35 ft rest-platform rule is 1926.451(e)(2)(iii)

facts.fact: Before entry, a permit-required confined space is tested in this order: oxygen content first, then flammable gases and vapors, then toxic air contaminants.

Safety nets must extend outward from the outermost projection of the work surface at least 8 ft when the drop is up to 5 ft, 10 ft when the drop is over 5 ft up to 10 ft, and 13 ft when the drop is over 10 ft.
Wire ropes on catenary scaffolds must be continuous, with no splices between anchors.
facts.reviewed: Catenary scaffolds are 1926.452(r) (rule is (r)(4)); (s) is float scaffolds

facts.fact: The assigned protection factor is 10 for a half-mask air-purifying respirator and 50 for a full-facepiece air-purifying respirator, so the full facepiece is rated 5 times as protective.
Compressed air may be used for cleaning only when reduced to less than 30 psi, and then only with effective chip guarding and proper PPE.

Personal fall arrest anchorages must be independent of anchorages supporting platforms and able to support at least 5,000 lb per attached employee, or be designed with a safety factor of at least two under a qualified person's supervision.
Under the Hazard Communication standard, employers must keep a Safety Data Sheet (SDS, formerly MSDS) for every hazardous chemical on site and make it readily available to workers during each shift.

Guardrail systems need midrails, screens, mesh or equivalent intermediate members between the top rail and the walking/working surface wherever there is no wall or parapet at least 21 in high; midrails go midway, and the top rail is 42 in plus or minus 3 in.

Jobsite housekeeping: form and scrap lumber with protruding nails and other debris must be kept clear of work areas, combustible scrap and debris must be removed at regular intervals, and scrap, waste and rubbish must be cleared from the immediate work area as the work progresses.

Jobsite first aid supplies must be kept in a weatherproof container with each item individually sealed, and the employer must check the kit before it goes out to each job and at least weekly so used or expired items are replaced.

Minimum jobsite toilets: 20 or fewer employees need 1 toilet; 20 or more employees need 1 toilet seat and 1 urinal per 40 workers; 200 or more need 1 toilet seat and 1 urinal per 50 workers. A crew of 25 therefore needs 1 toilet seat and 1 urinal.

OSHA permissible noise exposure (slow response): 90 dBA for 8 hours, 92 dBA for 6 hours, 95 dBA for 4 hours, 97 dBA for 3 hours, 100 dBA for 2 hours, 102 dBA for 1.5 hours, 105 dBA for 1 hour, 110 dBA for 0.5 hour and 115 dBA for 0.25 hour or less.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.52 Table D-2 (mixed exposure note)
facts.fact: For exposure at several noise levels, add each fraction of actual time divided by permitted time; a total greater than 1 exceeds the limit. Example: 1/4 h at 110 dBA (0.25/0.5) + 1/2 h at 105 dBA (0.5/1) + 3 h at 95 dBA (3/4) = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.75 = 1.75, which is over the limit.

OSHA Table D-3 minimum illumination: 5 foot-candles for 'general construction area lighting'; 3 foot-candles for 'general construction areas, concrete placement, excavation and waste areas, accessways, active storage areas, loading platforms, refueling and field maintenance areas'; 5 for indoor warehouses, corridors and exitways and for tunnels and general underground work; 10 for construction plants and shops; 30 for first aid stations, infirmaries and offices.
facts.note: Both the 5 fc and 3 fc rows mention general construction areas. Exam questions worded 'general construction area lighting' expect 5; items about construction areas listed with concrete placement or excavation expect 3.
facts.reviewed: Table D-3's 3 fc row actually begins 'General construction areas, concrete placement...'; the fact and note wrongly said the card was in error

facts.fact: Workers exposed to possible head injury from impact, falling or flying objects, or electrical shock and burns must wear protective helmets, and the employer is responsible for providing head protection that meets the ANSI Z89.1 standard.

When employees are exposed to eye or face hazards such as flying particles, molten metal, liquid chemicals, acids, caustic liquids or injurious light, the employer must provide eye and face protection.

A personal fall arrest system must use a full body harness (body belts are not allowed for fall arrest), lanyards and vertical lifelines with at least 5,000 lb breaking strength, and be rigged so the worker free falls no more than 6 ft and cannot contact any lower level; deceleration distance is limited to 3.5 ft and arresting force to 1,800 lb with a harness.
facts.note: Card says a safety belt lanyard must be at least 1/2-in nylon with a 6 ft maximum fall, which is the legacy safety-belt rule (old 1926.104). Body belts have been prohibited as part of a personal fall arrest system since January 1, 1998; current requirements are in 1926.502(d).

facts.fact: Safety nets must be installed as close as practicable below the work surface and never more than 30 ft below it, and must extend outward from the edge 8 ft when up to 5 ft below the work surface, 10 ft when more than 5 ft up to 10 ft below, and 13 ft when more than 10 ft below.

Safety net mesh openings may not exceed 36 sq in or 6 in on a side, connections between net panels must be as strong as the integral net components and spaced no more than 6 in apart, and nets must pass a drop test with a 400 lb bag of sand about 30 in in diameter.

Temporary heaters used in confined or enclosed spaces require sufficient ventilation for safe combustion and to protect workers, and heaters used near combustible tarpaulins, canvas or similar coverings must be at least 10 ft from them.

A radiant-type room heater needs at least 36 in clearance from combustible material above, in front, at the sides and at the rear; a circulating-type room heater needs 36 in above, 24 in in front and 12 in at the sides and rear.
Loose brick stacks may not exceed 7 ft in height, and once a stack reaches 4 ft it must be tapered back 2 in for every foot of height above the 4 ft level.
When masonry blocks are stacked higher than 6 ft, the stack must be tapered back one-half block per tier above the 6 ft level.
Used lumber must have all nails removed before stacking; lumber must be stacked on level, solidly supported sills, and piles may not exceed 20 ft high, or 16 ft if the lumber is handled manually.

Rigging equipment for material handling must be inspected before use on each shift and as needed during use, and defective rigging must be removed from service; slings and their fastenings and attachments must also be inspected each day before use by a competent person designated by the employer.
facts.reviewed: Merged two rules: (a)(1) per-shift inspection does not name a competent person; (a)(6) daily sling inspection by a competent person

facts.fact: An enclosed chute is required whenever material is dropped more than 20 ft to any point outside the exterior walls of the building.

When debris is dropped through floor holes without a chute, the drop area must be fully enclosed by barricades at least 42 in high set at least 6 ft back from the projected edge of the opening above, with warning signs posted at each level.
Power tools designed to accept guards must have those guards in place when in use; the point of operation is the area of a machine where work is actually performed on the material.

Hand-held tools such as drills, fastener drivers, grinders and disc sanders with wheels or discs over 2 in, belt sanders, reciprocating and saber saws, and jigsaws with blade shanks wider than 1/4 in need a momentary-contact on-off control, which may have a lock-on that releases with a single motion of the same finger; platen sanders, grinders and disc sanders 2 in or smaller, routers, planers and jigsaws with blade shanks 1/4 in or narrower may have only a positive on-off control.
facts.reviewed: Only jigsaws with blade shanks 1/4 in or narrower may have a positive on-off control; wider-shank jigsaws need momentary contact

facts.fact: Pneumatic nailers, staplers and similar tools operating above 100 psi must have a safety device on the muzzle to prevent ejecting fasteners unless the muzzle is against the work; compressed air for cleaning must be reduced below 30 psi and used only with effective chip guarding and personal protective equipment.

Only employees trained in the operation of the particular tool may operate a powder-actuated tool; the tool must be tested daily before loading and must not be loaded until just before use or left loaded unattended.

Floor-stand and bench-mounted abrasive wheels used for external grinding need safety guards (hoods), and the exposed wheel periphery and sides may not exceed 90 degrees, or 125 degrees when the work must contact the wheel below the horizontal plane of the spindle.
facts.reviewed: The 90/125 degree exposure limit is in 1926.303(c)(1)

facts.fact: Eye shields that provide adequate eye protection are often permanently mounted on the bench or floor stand of a grinder.
facts.note: Statement reflects common OSHA guidance on grinders, but the specific wording could not be tied to a regulatory paragraph; workers still need eye protection per 1926.102.

facts.fact: Portable power-driven circular saws need guards above and below the base plate: the upper guard covers the saw to the depth of the teeth except for the arc needed to tilt the base for bevel cuts, and the lower guard covers to the depth of the teeth and returns automatically to the covering position when the saw is withdrawn.

Compressed gas cylinders must be moved by tilting and rolling them on their bottom edges and must not be intentionally dropped or struck; valve protection caps may not be used to lift cylinders, and cylinders being hoisted must be secured on a cradle, slingboard or pallet, never lifted by magnets or choker slings.
facts.reviewed: 1926.350(a)(2) says cradle, slingboard or pallet; and cylinders 'shall' be moved by tilting and rolling

facts.fact: Stored oxygen cylinders must be separated from fuel-gas cylinders and combustible materials (especially oil or grease) by at least 20 ft or by a noncombustible barrier at least 5 ft high with a fire-resistance rating of at least one-half hour.

Gas cylinder valves must always be opened slowly to protect the regulator, fuel-gas cylinder valves should not be opened more than 1-1/2 turns, and a valve key or wrench must stay on the stem of non-handwheel valves while the cylinder is in use.
Hoses carrying acetylene, oxygen, fuel gas or any harmful substance must be inspected at the beginning of each working shift, and defective hose must be removed from service.
Whenever practicable, arc welding and cutting operations must be shielded with noncombustible or flameproof screens to protect nearby workers from the direct rays of the arc.

Oxygen must never be used to ventilate a welding area, and when a welder enters a confined space through a manhole or other small opening, lifelines or similar means must be provided for quick removal in an emergency, with an attendant stationed outside.

A catenary scaffold is a suspension scaffold whose platform rests on two essentially horizontal, parallel ropes attached to structural members; no more than one platform may be placed between consecutive vertical pickups and no more than two platforms may be used on one catenary scaffold.
Each scaffold and scaffold component must support its own weight plus at least 4 times the maximum intended load, and each suspension rope must support at least 6 times the maximum intended load.

Scaffold platforms must be fully planked or decked with gaps between units and between the platform and uprights no more than 1 in (unless a wider space is shown to be necessary), and work platforms must generally be at least 18 in wide.

Scaffolds and conductive material on them must stay at least 3 ft from insulated power lines under 300 volts and at least 10 ft from insulated lines of 300 V to 50 kV and from uninsulated lines under 50 kV; above 50 kV the distance is 10 ft plus 0.4 in for each kV over 50 kV.

On pole scaffolds, bearers must extend at least 3 in beyond the outside edges of the runners, and when a platform is moved to the next level the existing platform must stay in place until the new bearers are set and braced.
Platforms on ladder jack scaffolds may not be higher than 20 ft.
Crawling boards (chicken ladders) used for roof construction, repair or maintenance must extend from the roof peak to the eaves.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L Appendix A (s); 1926.452(s)(1)
facts.fact: OSHA's non-mandatory scaffold specifications describe float (ship) scaffolds for a maximum intended load of 750 lb; the mandatory rule requires at least two bearers extending at least 6 in beyond the platform on each side.
facts.reviewed: 1926.452(s) contains no load limit; 750 lb is from non-mandatory Appendix A to Subpart L

facts.fact: The employer must have each employee who works on a scaffold trained by a qualified person on its hazards; employees who erect, disassemble, move, operate, repair, maintain or inspect scaffolds must be trained by a competent person on the hazards, correct procedures, design criteria, maximum intended load and load-carrying capacity.
Workers on the face of formwork or reinforcing steel must be protected from falls of 6 ft or more by personal fall arrest systems, safety nets or positioning device systems.

During overhand bricklaying, an employee reaching more than 10 in below the level of the walking/working surface must be protected by guardrails, safety nets or personal fall arrest, and no materials other than masonry and mortar may be stored within 4 ft of the working edge.
facts.reviewed: The 4 ft overhand bricklaying storage rule is 1926.502(j)(6)

facts.fact: Guardrail top rails must be 42 in plus or minus 3 in above the walking/working level and withstand 200 lb; midrails, screens or mesh are needed when there is no wall or parapet at least 21 in high, with midrails set midway between the top rail and the surface and able to withstand 150 lb.
Horizontal lifelines must be designed, installed and used under the supervision of a qualified person as part of a complete personal fall arrest system that maintains a safety factor of at least two.

Lanyards and vertical lifelines must have a minimum breaking strength of 5,000 lb, and anchorages for personal fall arrest must support at least 5,000 lb per attached employee or be designed by a qualified person with a safety factor of at least two.

Only locking-type snaphooks may be used in personal fall arrest systems, and they may not be hooked directly to webbing, rope, each other or an incompatible object unless designed for it; fall arrest systems must not be attached to guardrail systems or to hoists except as specifically allowed.

Personal fall arrest systems must be inspected before each use for wear, damage and deterioration, defective components must be removed from service, and any system that has arrested a fall must be taken out of service until a competent person inspects it.

Roof warning lines are made of ropes, wires or chains on supporting stanchions, flagged with high-visibility material at no more than 6 ft intervals, with the line between 34 in and 39 in above the surface and at least 6 ft back from the roof edge (10 ft perpendicular to the direction of mechanical equipment).

Covers over holes in floors, roofs and other walking surfaces must support at least twice the weight of employees, equipment and materials that may be on them, be secured against displacement, and be marked HOLE or COVER (or color coded).

During roofing work, materials and equipment may not be stored within 6 ft of a roof edge unless guardrails are erected at that edge, and stacked materials near the edge must be stable and self-supporting.
facts.reviewed: Roofing storage rule is 1926.502(j)(7)
