facts.fact: Employers must train every employee exposed to fall hazards through a competent person, document it with a written certification record showing the employee name, training date and signature of the trainer or employer, and retrain when changes or observed deficiencies show it is needed.
Personnel hoist towers located outside the structure must be enclosed for the full height on the side or sides used for entering and exiting the structure.

Cranes working near power lines must keep the equipment, load line and load at least 20 ft from lines up to 350 kV (50 ft above 350 kV) unless the utility confirms the voltage; with the voltage known, Table A minimums apply: 10 ft up to 50 kV, 15 ft over 50 to 200 kV, 20 ft over 200 to 350 kV, 25 ft over 350 to 500 kV.
facts.note: Card cites Subpart O 1926.600 (and the former 1926.550 crane rule) for a 10 ft clearance up to 50 kV. Cranes and derricks are now covered by Subpart CC (1926.1408); 10 ft still applies up to 50 kV when the voltage is confirmed, but the default is 20 ft when it is not.

facts.fact: OSHA 1926.602(a)(5) calls for fenders on all wheels of pneumatic-tired earthmoving haulage equipment (trucks, scrapers, tractors and trailing units) with a maximum speed over 15 mph, but OSHA has suspended that fender requirement pending reconsideration.
facts.reviewed: Rule is 1926.602(a)(5), and the fender requirement is suspended pending reconsideration by 1926.602(a)(8)(ii)

facts.fact: Equipment used in site clearing must have rollover guards meeting Subpart W, and rider-operated equipment also needs an overhead and rear canopy guard.

When sloping or benching is designed from tabulated data, at least one copy of that data, identifying the registered professional engineer who approved it, must be kept at the jobsite during construction of the protective system.

In trenches protected by shield systems, earth may be excavated up to 2 ft below the bottom of the shield only if the shield is designed for the forces of the full trench depth and there is no sign of soil loss from behind or below it.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A
facts.fact: Soil classification uses both visual analysis and manual tests; manual tests include the plasticity (thread) test, dry strength test, thumb penetration test, pocket penetrometer or shearvane strength tests, and the drying test.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B Table B-1
facts.fact: Maximum allowable slopes for excavations 20 ft deep or less: stable rock vertical (90 degrees), Type A soil 3/4:1 (53 degrees), Type B soil 1:1 (45 degrees), Type C soil 1-1/2:1 (34 degrees), stated as horizontal to vertical.

Masonry walls over 8 ft high must be braced to prevent overturning and collapse unless otherwise adequately supported, and a limited access zone equal to the wall height plus 4 ft must be set up along the full length of the wall on the unscaffolded side.

A steel erection contractor may not begin erecting steel until it receives written notification that the concrete in footings, piers and walls has reached 75 percent of its intended minimum compressive design strength (based on ASTM tests of field-cured samples) or enough strength to carry erection loads.
Steel erection columns must be anchored by at least 4 anchor rods (anchor bolts).

On open web steel joists that require bolted diagonal erection bridging, hoisting cables may not be released until that bridging is installed and anchored; only one employee is allowed on spans that need a single midspan row (per Tables A and B) and no more than two employees on 60 to 144 ft spans until all bridging is installed and anchored.
facts.reviewed: Erection-bridging rules are in 1926.757(d)(1)-(3), not (c)(5)-(7)

facts.fact: Steel erection workers on surfaces with unprotected sides or edges more than 15 ft above a lower level need fall protection, while connectors and workers in a controlled decking zone get protection at more than two stories or 30 ft, whichever is less.
In underground construction the employer must keep a check-in/check-out procedure so aboveground personnel can accurately count the people underground in an emergency.

Underground work areas must get enough fresh air to prevent dangerous accumulations of dusts, fumes, mists, vapors or gases, with at least 200 cubic feet per minute of fresh air for each employee underground.
Before demolition begins, a competent person must make an engineering survey of the structure to assess the condition of its framing, floors and walls and the possibility of unplanned collapse.
A stairway or ladder is required at any break in elevation of 19 in or more with no ramp or other safe access, and stairs must be installed between 30 and 50 degrees from horizontal.

Side rails of through and side-step fixed ladders must extend 42 in above the top of the access level or landing; for a parapet ladder the access level is the roof if the parapet is cut for passage, or the top of the parapet if it is continuous.
The top cap or top step of a stepladder may not be used as a step.

In the OSHA construction asbestos standard, asbestos means chrysotile, amosite, crocidolite, tremolite, anthophyllite and actinolite asbestos, including chemically treated or altered forms, and PACM is presumed asbestos-containing material; the exposure limits are 0.1 fiber/cc as an 8-hour TWA and 1.0 fiber/cc averaged over 30 minutes (excursion limit).

The employer must provide, and require the use of, protective clothing such as coveralls for any employee exposed to airborne asbestos above the TWA or excursion limit, or doing certain classes of asbestos work.
A confined space is large enough for an employee to enter and work, has limited or restricted means of entry or exit, and is not designed for continuous employee occupancy.

Before entry, a confined space atmosphere must be tested with a calibrated direct-reading instrument in this order: oxygen content first, then flammable gases and vapors, then potential toxic air contaminants.

facts.source: SBCA/TPI BCSI-B1; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC
facts.fact: BCSI guidance places responsibility for crane compliance with OSHA on the crane operator and/or contractor unless a contract expressly assigns it to someone else.
facts.note: Allocation of responsibility is contractual and comes from handbook guidance; under OSHA Subpart CC duties fall on the employer operating the equipment and on the controlling entity, so check the contract.

facts.fact: When a crane manufacturer's procedures are unavailable, the employer must develop them: operational control procedures by a qualified person, and procedures related to capacity (equipment limitations) developed and signed by a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment.

Before excavating in Georgia, a contractor must contact Georgia 811 (the Utilities Protection Center). The cards say utility owners have 48 hours, excluding non-business days, to mark their facilities.
facts.note: State-specific; Georgia's locate response period and ticket rules have been amended. Confirm the current number of business days.

facts.fact: Where a gravel or crushed-stone foundation drain is required, the drainage material must extend at least 12 in beyond the outside edge of the footing and its top must be at least 6 in above the top of the footing.
The raised ribs (deformations) on reinforcing bars are made on purpose to improve bond, so the concrete grips the steel and load transfers between them.
Connections in precast concrete frames are usually treated as pinned, so they resist little moment; lateral stability must come from shear walls, bracing or other lateral systems.
facts.note: Card says pin-type connections provide lateral stability. Pinned connections do not resist moment, so stability has to be provided by a separate lateral system.

facts.fact: A topographic survey shows existing ground contours and elevations; the sitework contractor compares it to design grades to figure cut and fill.

Footings must be stepped where the top elevation changes or where a slope steeper than 1 vertical in 10 horizontal (10%) occurs: under the IRC, where the bottom of the footing would slope more than 10%; under the IBC, where the ground surface slopes more than 10%.
facts.reviewed: IRC trigger is the footing bottom slope; IBC 1809.3 trigger is the ground surface slope; fact applied the IRC wording to both

facts.fact: Deep foundation elements standing unbraced in air, water or fluid soils may be considered laterally supported at a point 5 ft into stiff soil or 10 ft into soft soil unless otherwise approved.
Structural steel H-piles must have a nominal depth in the direction of the web of at least 8 in, flange and web thickness of at least 3/8 in, and flange width at least 80% of the section depth.

For an embedded post or pole, the hole must be at least 4 in larger than the column's diameter at its bottom, or 4 in larger than the diagonal of a square or rectangular column, to leave room for backfill.
Cast-in-place or grouted-in-place deep foundation elements must have a diameter of at least 12 in without a permanent casing, or a nominal outside diameter of at least 8 in with a permanent casing.
The foundation or superstructure must be designed to handle a deep foundation element being out of position by at least 3 in.
Prestressed members are unloaded in their upright (as-cast service) orientation and lifted and supported at points near their ends unless other points are designated.
facts.note: From precast industry (PCI) handling guidance; cannot confirm exact wording against the source.

facts.fact: When stacking stemmed members or hollow-core plank, dunnage should not run continuously across more than one stack of precast units.
facts.note: Precast industry storage guidance; cannot confirm against the source document.

facts.fact: Drypack is mortar mixed with just enough water to make a stiff, damp, crumbly material that is rammed or packed into place, often under base plates or in voids.
Vertical placement tolerance for post-tensioning tendons in members 8 to 24 in deep is plus or minus 3/8 in (plus or minus 1/4 in for members 8 in or less, and 1/2 in for members over 24 in).
If a post-tensioning tendon breaks during stressing, the decision on whether it must be replaced is made by the engineer of record working with the post-tensioning supplier.
facts.note: Reflects PTI practice; project specifications decide who has authority, and the engineer of record normally has final say.

facts.fact: Enough tendon tail must be left beyond the slab edge at each stressing end for the jack to grip; a figure of about 12 in per end is often quoted for a tendon stressed at both ends.
facts.note: Required tail length depends on the stressing jack and the supplier's procedures; could not confirm a fixed 12 in value.

facts.fact: Percent slope is rise divided by run times 100, so a 100% slope has equal rise and run and corresponds to a 45-degree angle.

Wellpoint dewatering works best in sands and gravels; in fine-grained silts and clays it is much less effective because water drains too slowly, so other methods (vacuum wellpoints, electro-osmosis) may be needed.
Grades are signed by direction of travel: an uphill grade is positive and a downhill grade is negative.
A nuclear density gauge measures in-place soil density and moisture quickly without removing a soil sample from the site, unlike sand-cone or rubber-balloon tests.
Coarse-grained soils such as gravel and sand drain freely and keep most of their strength when saturated, whereas fine-grained silts and clays lose strength and become unworkable when wet.

Coarse sand and gravel compact best with vibration (vibratory rollers or plates) and adequate water, while cohesive clays compact best with kneading or impact equipment such as sheepsfoot or padfoot rollers.

The thrust at a pipe bend equals 2 x internal pressure x pipe cross-sectional area x sin(bend angle / 2), and the required thrust block bearing area equals that thrust divided by the allowable soil bearing pressure.
Bull floating right after screeding levels ridges, fills low spots and pushes coarse aggregate just below the surface, and it must be finished before bleed water appears.

Saturated silt or clay well above optimum moisture cannot be properly compacted; it must be dried by aeration or discing, stabilized with lime or cement, or removed and replaced with suitable dry fill.
Slot dozing pushes material down the same path repeatedly so the trench walls keep soil from spilling off the blade, reducing load loss during the push.
Tracked backhoes or excavators are preferred for trenching in soft soil because tracks spread the machine's weight (lower ground pressure) and give better traction and stability than wheels.
The angle of repose of compacted sharp sand is often listed at about 33 degrees.
facts.note: Handbook value; reported angles for sand vary with grading, moisture and compaction.

facts.fact: Concrete flatwork is finished in this order: screed (strike off) to grade, bull float, wait for bleed water to leave, then edge and joint, float, and finally trowel.

facts.source: Standard construction practice; IRC 2021 R608 (ICF walls)
facts.fact: Insulating concrete forms (ICFs), hollow foam blocks or panels filled with reinforced concrete, are stay-in-place forms that remain as part of the finished wall and provide its insulation.
Shear in a concrete beam causes diagonal tension cracking, which usually starts near the supports at about 45 degrees; stirrups (shear reinforcement) are placed to resist it.
An inch-pound rebar number is its nominal diameter in eighths of an inch, so a #4 bar is 1/2 in (0.50 in) and a #6 bar is 3/4 in (0.75 in) in diameter.
ACI 117 allows stirrup spacing to vary by about plus or minus 1 in, as long as the total number of stirrups is not reduced.
facts.note: Card says 1 inch. I believe this matches ACI 117, but tolerance tables have changed between editions and I cannot confirm the current wording.

facts.fact: Under the Unified Soil Classification System, sand is soil that passes the No. 4 sieve (4.75 mm) but is retained on the No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm); coarser is gravel and finer is silt or clay.

facts.source: Principles and Practices of Commercial Construction (NASCLA reference text)
facts.fact: A NASCLA reference textbook is reported to list dense silt as suitable for roughly 3,000 psf (about 140 kPa) of estimated foundation bearing pressure, which differs from the IBC presumptive value for silts.
facts.note: Cards 355 and 363 answer dense silt for 3,000 psf / 140 kPa. Under IBC/IRC presumptive values silts get only 1,500 psf and 3,000 psf is for gravel. The textbook table could not be confirmed; students should know both.

facts.fact: Expansive (clay) soils change volume with moisture, swelling when they get wet and shrinking as they dry, which can heave or crack foundations and slabs.
Where a sidewalk bears against a building or other fixed structure, isolation/expansion joints are provided there and at intervals along the walk, commonly cited as no more than about 30 ft apart.
facts.note: Card says 30 ft maximum. This comes from a textbook or agency specification and varies by jurisdiction; not a model-code requirement.

facts.fact: Sheet piles are interlocking sections driven to form a wall that resists lateral (horizontal) earth and water pressure, as in cofferdams and excavation support; they are generally not used as the primary support for vertical building loads.
facts.reviewed: Overstated; steel sheet piles are sometimes designed to carry vertical load (e.g., bridge abutments)

facts.fact: Shoring may be removed only after the structure has enough strength to carry its loads, shown by tests of field-cured cylinders or another approved method of estimating in-place strength.
Concrete must be kept above 50 degrees F and moist for at least the first 7 days after placement, or at least the first 3 days for high-early-strength concrete, unless accelerated curing is used.
facts.reviewed: Curing durations are in the construction requirements (26.5.3.2), not 26.5.3.1

facts.fact: In beams of special (seismic) moment frames, hoops are required near each end of the beam, and the first hoop must be no more than 2 in from the face of the supporting column.
facts.note: Card asks about a column connected to a wall. The 2-in first-hoop rule in ACI 318 applies to beams framing into a supporting column in special moment frames.

facts.fact: A typical square or rectangular spread footing is a slab of uniform thickness with its main reinforcing bars near the bottom (tension) face, running in both directions.

Formwork for an elevated slab is designed for the slab's dead load plus a construction live load of at least 50 psf (75 psf if motorized carts are used), and the combined design load must be at least 100 psf (125 psf with motorized carts).
Field and lab quality-control tests on concrete follow ASTM standards: slump (C143), air content (C231 or C173), making and testing strength cylinders (C31 and C39), and unit weight and yield (C138).

facts.source: PCA Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (air entrainment)
facts.fact: Entrained air improves freeze-thaw resistance, but too much air lowers compressive strength (roughly 5% per extra percentage point of air), so air content is held within the specified range.
Camber is building formwork slightly upward so that when wet concrete loads it and the forms deflect, the finished member ends up at the intended elevation.
Duplex (double-headed) nails are used for temporary work such as form bracing because the upper head stays exposed and can be pulled easily when the forms are stripped.
Lateral pressure on wall and column forms goes up with faster placement, deeper lifts, cooler concrete and retarded mixes, so slowing the rate of placement is the main field method of reducing it.

facts.source: ACI 306R cold weather concreting; ACI 318 chloride limits
facts.fact: In cold weather an accelerating admixture is added to speed setting and early strength; calcium chloride is the traditional accelerator (generally no more than 2% by weight of cement), but it is limited or prohibited in reinforced, prestressed, or aluminum-embedded concrete because chlorides cause corrosion.
Lightly dampening a dry subgrade before placing concrete stops it from quickly drawing mixing water out of the concrete; there should be no standing water or mud.

facts.source: ACI 305R hot weather concreting; ACI 232 fly ash
facts.fact: Replacing part of the cement with fly ash lowers and slows the heat of hydration, which helps in hot weather and mass pours; usual hot-weather measures also include retarders, chilled water or ice, and never adding water to the mix.
facts.note: Card says fly ash is used to cool concrete that contains too much water. Fly ash reduces heat of hydration; it is not a remedy for excess water, which lowers strength and must be prevented.

facts.fact: A set-retarding admixture slows setting so that hot concrete stays workable long enough to place and finish properly.
Admixtures are used for things like controlling set time, reducing water, entraining air and improving workability and durability; they are used to decrease permeability, never to increase it.
Higher concrete temperature shortens setting and finishing time sharply; one cited rule of thumb is that a 20 degree F increase cuts finishing time by about half.
facts.note: Card says a 20 degree F increase reduces finishing time by 50%. Published rules of thumb vary (some say about one-third per 20 degrees F); could not confirm the exact ACI figure.

facts.source: Fiber tube column form manufacturer guidance
facts.fact: Laminated fiber (cardboard tube) column forms need external bracing to stay plumb, with one cited threshold being forms taller than about 15 ft.
facts.note: Card says brace if over 15 ft. Bracing requirements come from manufacturer instructions and vary by diameter and conditions.

facts.source: ASTM C494 Types F and G
facts.fact: High-range water-reducing admixtures (superplasticizers) greatly increase slump without extra water, or allow large water reductions for high-strength concrete.
Gang forms are large panels assembled from smaller ones and moved by crane as a unit, which gives high reuse, covers large placements, and cuts erection time.
Contraction (control) joints in slabs on grade should be cut to at least one-quarter of the slab thickness, for example 1-1/4 in deep in a 5-in slab.

facts.source: CRSI / AWS D1.4 guidance on tack welding reinforcing bars
facts.fact: Tack welding reinforcing bars (for example to hold bars in place) can seriously weaken them, so it is not allowed unless approved by the engineer and done under AWS D1.4; one cited figure puts the reduced capacity at 35-40% of original.
facts.note: Card says 35-40%. The weakening effect is real, but the specific percentage could not be confirmed and varies with bar chemistry and welding procedure.

facts.fact: Type III portland cement is high-early-strength cement, used when concrete must gain strength fast, for example to strip forms early or in cold weather; Type I is general purpose, Type II moderate sulfate resistance, Type IV low heat, and Type V high sulfate resistance.
Dry-pack mortar (a stiff, low-water mix rammed into place) is used to fill joints and spaces such as under base plates, with about 1 in commonly cited as the governing joint thickness.
facts.note: Card says joints for drypack should be at least 1 in thick. Sources differ on whether 1 in is a minimum or maximum for dry-pack versus flowable grout; could not confirm.

facts.source: PCA Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures
facts.fact: Concrete is a mixture of portland cement, fine and coarse aggregate and water; portland cement is made by heating limestone and clay or shale in a kiln to form clinker, which is ground with gypsum.

facts.source: PCA Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures
facts.fact: Aggregates make up about 60 to 75 percent of concrete volume and their quality and grading affect strength, but the water-cement ratio is the main factor controlling strength, durability and watertightness; adding water without cement lowers strength (it does not control color).
Retarding admixtures slow the setting of concrete (useful in hot weather), while accelerating admixtures speed setting and early strength gain (useful in cold weather).
The slump test measures concrete consistency: the greater the slump, the wetter and more fluid the mix.
facts.note: Card answer is garbled (it repeats 'color and aesthetics'). A higher slump indicates a wetter mix.

facts.fact: Consolidation removes trapped air from fresh concrete; on small jobs it is done by hand rodding, spading, tamping or tapping the forms, while larger placements use mechanical vibrators.
A dumpy (builder's) level is described in carpentry texts as the simplest and least expensive optical leveling instrument compared with a transit-level.
facts.note: Relative cost claim is textbook-specific and depends on what instruments are compared (hand levels and water levels are cheaper still).

facts.fact: A benchmark is a reference point of known elevation used to lay out a building and set grades; the rod holder raises or lowers the target until it aligns with the instrument crosshair, and a larger rod reading means lower ground (readings of 5 ft at A and 7 ft at B mean B is 2 ft lower).
In angle measurement, one degree equals 60 minutes and one minute equals 60 seconds.
A rectangular building can be laid out without an instrument using two long tapes: square corners are checked with the 3-4-5 triangle method and by confirming both diagonals are equal.

Batter boards are horizontal boards nailed to stakes set outside the building corners so string lines can mark the building lines after excavation; their tops are often set at the height of the foundation wall.

A footing is the widened base of a foundation that spreads the building load over a larger area of soil; form ties such as snap ties hold the two sides of wall forms together and are snapped off after the forms are stripped.

Steel joist placement plans must show loads, nonstandard joist profiles, support and splice connections, deflection criteria, bridging size and location, and joist headers, but they do not need the seal and signature of the joist manufacturer's registered design professional.
Trusses are to be set close to their plan locations along the bearing; one cited tolerance is within 1/4 in of the dimension shown.
facts.note: Industry installation guide value; could not confirm the exact tolerance figure.

facts.fact: Lifting guidance for trusses depends on span: shorter trusses (around 30 ft) may be lifted at one or two pick points with taglines, while longer trusses need spreader bars and more pick points.
facts.note: Cards conflict (one says 1 pick point for parallel-chord trusses up to 30 ft, another says 2 points for 30 ft single trusses); exact counts depend on truss type in BCSI diagrams.

facts.fact: Temporary lateral restraint and bracing for trusses is attached to each truss with at least two 16d nails.
facts.note: Industry guide (BCSI) recommendation rather than code; nail specifications may vary by edition.

facts.fact: In a two-leg bridle, each leg carries (load / 2) / sin(angle from horizontal). At 45 degrees each leg carries about 0.707 times the total load, so a 50,000 lb lift puts about 35,400 lb on each leg; size the rope from the rated-capacity tables.
Steel joists should be stored on site upright, in the position they were shipped, on blocking off the ground so they do not bend, twist or collect water.
facts.note: Manufacturer/SJI handling recommendation rather than a code requirement.

facts.fact: When steel joists bear on a joist girder, they must be located at the girder's top-chord panel points, because joist girders are designed to receive concentrated loads only there.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.757; SJI Code of Standard Practice
facts.fact: Before any field modification of a steel joist or joist girder, consult the joist manufacturer; OSHA prohibits modifications that affect joist strength without written approval of the project structural engineer of record.
For composite floors on formed steel deck, the concrete must be at least 2 in thick above the top of the deck flutes.

facts.source: Cold-formed steel framing practice (AISI S240 / manufacturer details)
facts.fact: When cold-formed steel track must be spliced, a short piece of track or stud is nested inside and fastened so it laps each side of the joint; a minimum splice length of about 6 in is commonly cited.
facts.note: Card says 6 in minimum track splice. Splice details depend on the AISI standard, manufacturer and engineer's details; could not confirm a single code minimum.

facts.source: Principles and Practices of Commercial Construction (metal panel systems)
facts.fact: Metal wall or roof panels designed as stressed-skin panels need no separate subframe and are attached directly to the building's structural frame, reportedly by clips.
facts.note: Card says clips. Attachment method depends on the panel system (clips or through-fasteners); could not confirm the textbook source.

facts.fact: In a pre-engineered metal building, rigid frames give stability across the width (transverse), while diagonal rod or cable (X) bracing in the roof and sidewalls gives longitudinal stability.

facts.source: SDI / AWS D1.3 (welding sheet steel deck)
facts.fact: Weld washers are required when arc spot (puddle) welding steel deck thinner than 0.028 in (about 22 gauge), because thin sheet would otherwise burn through.
Steel floor deck used as a working platform during construction must be able to support specified construction loads, with one cited minimum of 50 psf uniform.
facts.note: Card says 50 psf. SDI construction-load criteria (uniform and concentrated loads) vary by standard edition; could not confirm the exact figure.

facts.fact: Trusses stored on site, especially for more than a week, should rest on blocking high enough to keep them off the ground, typically at 8 to 10 ft intervals, to limit lateral bending and moisture pickup, and should be covered for weather protection.
facts.note: Interval comes from BCSI industry handbook guidance; confirm with the current BCSI-B1 summary sheet and the truss manufacturer's instructions.

facts.fact: Lift trusses with closed-loop attachments (slings, chains, straps) on the top chord, control them with tag lines, and avoid lateral (out-of-plane) bending, which can damage plates and members; erection should stop in high winds or lightning.

Single trusses up to 30 ft long are lifted with at least 2 pick points near top chord joints spaced no more than about half the truss length apart; trusses over 60 ft need a strongback or spreader bar about 2/3 to 3/4 of the truss length.
Trusses roughly 30 to 60 ft long should be lifted with a spreader bar about 1/2 to 2/3 of the truss length, attached at the top chord.
facts.note: Card says a spreader bar 1/2 to 1/3 of the truss length. BCSI-B1 calls for about 1/2 to 2/3 in this range; the card's 1/3 appears garbled and would be shorter than the pick spacing used for trusses under 30 ft.

facts.fact: The first truss set must be securely attached to ground bracing (exterior or interior) and braced before others are added, because every following truss depends on it for stability.

Unless the building designer specifies otherwise, temporary lateral restraint and diagonal bracing should be at least 2x4 stress-graded lumber attached to each truss with at least two 16d nails (or equivalent).
When the first truss cannot be ground braced from the building exterior, it may be set and braced from the interior, sometimes starting near the middle of the building.
facts.note: Card says install it in the center of the building; BCSI shows interior ground bracing options but the exact location depends on site conditions and the designer's bracing plan.

facts.fact: Installation tolerances in handbook guidance: for top chord bearing parallel chord trusses, the gap between the inside edge of the bearing and the first web should not exceed 1/2 in, and truss spacing along the bearing should be within about plus or minus 1/4 in of plan.
facts.note: Specific tolerances come from BCSI/truss manufacturer guidance and could not be confirmed against a code; check the truss design drawings.

facts.fact: Trusses must be set at their exact design spacing before lateral restraints and diagonal bracing are fastened, and construction should not proceed until the bracing is securely in place.
Never stack materials on unbraced trusses; once braced, place only limited amounts that will not overload them, positioned over or next to load-bearing walls rather than near midspan.
Lateral restraints by themselves can let trusses shift together, so rows of lateral restraint must be anchored with diagonal bracing.
Before erecting trusses, confirm the building dimensions match the trusses, bearing walls and supports are plumb and braced, and the tops of bearings are at the correct elevation.
Web member plane diagonal bracing is installed to stabilize the first five trusses, with braces crossing the web members at roughly 45 degrees.
Diagonal bracing is required at each end of the building and repeated every 10 truss spaces, with no more than 20 ft between diagonal braces along continuous top chord lateral restraint.
BCTLR means bottom chord temporary lateral restraint; rows are installed at a maximum of 15 ft on center.

A hip set is a series of trusses that step down in height to form the sloped end of a hip roof; a valley set is a group of trusses that sits on top of other trusses to change the direction of roof planes.
Trusses overstressed by excessive construction loads may suffer broken members, failed joints, or permanent sag that remains after the load is removed.

Truss members must never be cut, drilled or altered without approval; problems or damage go to the building designer, truss designer or truss manufacturer, and approved repairs typically use plywood or OSB gussets, metal nail-on plates, or lumber scabs over broken chords or webs.

Permanent bracing is required in the top chord plane, bottom chord plane and web member plane; it prevents out-of-plane buckling of compression members, keeps trusses properly spaced, and transfers lateral loads; diagonal bracing in the web plane at the building ends and at designer-specified intervals is called sway bracing.
Each end of a ceiling joist or rafter must have at least 1-1/2 in of bearing on wood or metal and at least 3 in of bearing on masonry or concrete.
Dry dimension lumber is smaller than its nominal size: a 2x4 is 1-1/2 x 3-1/2 in, 2x6 is 1-1/2 x 5-1/2 in, 2x8 is 1-1/2 x 7-1/4 in, 2x10 is 1-1/2 x 9-1/4 in and 2x12 is 1-1/2 x 11-1/4 in.
Unseasoned (green) 2x6 lumber is dressed to 1-9/16 x 5-5/8 in, so it is 3/8 in narrower than a 6 in steel stud.
A pocket door frame must be installed during framing, before the drywall, because the door slides into a cavity inside the wall.

Notches at the ends of solid lumber joists may not exceed 1/4 of the joist depth; notches elsewhere are limited to 1/6 of the depth, no longer than 1/3 of the depth, and not in the middle third of the span.

Preservative-treated wood must bear an approved quality mark identifying the treating manufacturer, inspection agency, preservative, minimum retention, applicable AWPA standard and intended end use (such as ground contact or foundation), plus moisture content if dried after treatment.

Untreated wood is allowed in locations that otherwise require treatment when it is continuously and entirely below the groundwater level or fully submerged in fresh water, because decay organisms cannot survive without oxygen.
facts.note: Exact code location of this exception not confirmed; verify the current IBC/IRC section before relying on the citation.
facts.reviewed: Concept is sound (similar exceptions exist, e.g. timber below permanent water level), but the cited IBC 2304.12 / IRC R317.1 wording could not be confirmed

facts.fact: Fasteners, nuts and washers in contact with preservative-treated wood, and those in fire-retardant-treated wood used outdoors or in wet or damp locations, must be hot-dipped zinc-coated galvanized steel, stainless steel, silicon bronze or copper. Limited exceptions apply, such as plain steel bolts 1/2 in diameter or larger, and FRT wood used indoors follows the manufacturer's recommendations.
facts.reviewed: For fire-retardant-treated wood the rule applies only to exterior or wet/damp use, and preservative-treated wood has exceptions (1/2 in or larger steel bolts, mechanically galvanized fasteners for some uses)

facts.fact: Floor openings are framed with trimmer joists and header joists carrying the cut tail joists; when the header span exceeds 4 ft the trimmers and header must be doubled, hangers are required where the header span exceeds 6 ft, and tail joists over 12 ft long need framing anchors or 2x2 ledger strips.

Where roof trusses or rafters bear on an exterior wall top plate, the connection must resist wind uplift (and lateral thrust); when calculated uplift exceeds what toenails provide, approved connectors such as hurricane ties are required.
Combination subfloor-underlayment 3/4 in thick or less (including 5/8 in) is fastened to framing with 8d common nails or 6d deformed-shank nails, spaced 6 in at panel edges and 12 in in the field.
A biscuit (plate) jointer is a portable power tool that cuts crescent-shaped slots in the edges of workpieces to receive wooden biscuits for alignment and gluing.
Lumber shrinkage along its length is negligible; nearly all shrinkage occurs across the width and thickness as the wood dries below the fiber saturation point.

facts.source: USDA Wood Handbook; lumber grading rules
facts.fact: A shake is a lengthwise grain separation between or through the growth rings; sapwood of native species has low natural decay resistance regardless of species.
Structural plywood grade trademarks are often stamped on the back face of the panel.
facts.note: Stamp location varies by panel type and mill (sheathing panels often carry the mark on the face, sanded panels on the back or edge).

facts.fact: OSB (oriented strand board) is made of wood strands bonded with adhesive under heat and pressure; wood structural panels such as plywood and OSB should be installed with about 1/8 in spacing at panel edges and ends to allow for expansion.
Glulam beams are often made with a slight upward curve called camber to offset deflection, and they must not be notched or drilled unless the design accounts for it.
A shear wall is a wall designed to resist lateral forces such as wind and seismic loads, and a girder is a large horizontal member that supports floor joists.
A nail's penny (d) size indicates its length: 8d is 2-1/2 in, 10d is 3 in and 16d is 3-1/2 in.
A tail joist is a shortened floor joist that runs from a header at an opening to a bearing wall or girder.
A gable is the triangular wall section formed by the sloping ends of a roof, and rafter slope is figured using a unit run of 12 in (unit rise per 12 in of run).

facts.source: Georgia State Licensing Board for Residential and General Contractors rules
facts.fact: Georgia contractor license applicants must show proof of general liability insurance (and workers' compensation where required); the card set gives minimums of $300,000 for residential and $500,000 for general (commercial) contractor applicants.
facts.note: State-specific board rule amounts could not be confirmed against current Georgia rules.

facts.fact: Insurance is a risk-transfer tool: in exchange for a premium, the insurer assumes the financial consequences of covered losses such as accidents, fire or theft.
Commercial property insurance covers a business's buildings and business personal property (equipment, inventory, furniture) against covered losses such as fire, theft and vandalism.

Builder's risk insurance covers a structure while it is under construction, including materials, supplies, fixtures and machinery that are or will become part of the building. An all-risk (special form) policy covers every peril not specifically excluded, while a named-peril policy covers only the perils listed, such as fire, lightning or windstorm.

Inland marine floaters cover movable property: a contractor's equipment floater covers mobile equipment and tools against physical loss whether stored, in transit or at a jobsite, and a transit (transportation) floater covers goods while being shipped.

Commercial general liability (CGL) insurance covers the contractor's legal liability for bodily injury and property damage suffered by third parties (people not employed by the company), subject to listed exclusions; injuries to the contractor's own employees are covered by workers' compensation instead.

An umbrella liability policy pays claims that exceed the limits of the underlying general liability (and auto/employer's liability) policies. A business owner's policy (BOP) bundles property and general liability coverage for small businesses.

Professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance protects against claims from design errors or oversights; directors and officers (D&O) insurance protects company directors and officers against claims of wrongful acts in performing their duties; key person insurance is life/disability coverage on an individual whose loss would seriously harm the company.

Workers' compensation provides medical care and partial wage replacement to employees with work-related injuries or illnesses regardless of fault. The employer pays the premium; employees contribute nothing in nearly all states (Washington is a notable exception with an employee payroll share).

facts.source: Contract law fundamentals (indemnification and contractual liability coverage)
facts.fact: Before signing a contract with a clause requiring the contractor to indemnify the owner, the contractor should review its liability insurance to confirm that contractual liability for that indemnity is covered.

A contract surety bond is a three-party agreement in which the surety guarantees to the obligee (owner) that the principal (contractor) will meet its obligations; unlike insurance, the contractor must reimburse the surety for any losses paid.

A bid bond assures the owner that the bidder submitted its bid in good faith and, if awarded, will sign the contract at the bid price and furnish the required performance and payment bonds. On federal contracts the bid guarantee must be at least 20% of the bid price, not to exceed $3 million.

A performance bond guarantees the contractor will complete the work according to the contract's terms, time and conditions; a payment bond guarantees that subcontractors and suppliers will be paid for labor and materials they furnish. A general contractor can protect against a subcontractor's non-performance by requiring a subcontract performance bond.

A maintenance bond guarantees that no defects in workmanship or materials will appear in the completed project for a stated period; a completion bond assures the project's lender or financial backers that the work will be finished on time and free of liens.

The Miller Act (enacted 1935) requires performance and payment bonds on federal construction contracts; the current FAR threshold is contracts exceeding $150,000. States have similar public-works bonding laws known as 'Little Miller Acts'.
facts.note: Card says the Miller Act applies to federal projects valued at $100,000. That was the statutory figure, but it has been inflation-adjusted to $150,000 in FAR 28.102-1; the October 2025 FAR inflation adjustment excluded the bond threshold, so $150,000 still applies.

facts.fact: On federal construction contracts, the performance bond and the payment bond are each normally 100% of the original contract price; the contracting officer may set a lower payment bond only if 100% is impractical, and never below the performance bond amount.
facts.note: Cards say a $5.1 million contract needs a $2.5 million payment bond and a $2.6 million contract needs a 40% ($1,040,000) payment bond. Those are the pre-1999 Miller Act sliding-scale amounts; the Construction Industry Payment Protection Act of 1999 and FAR 28.102-2(b) set payment bonds at 100% of contract price.

facts.fact: Workers' compensation covers employees who are injured or become ill from their work, regardless of fault, and generally does not cover independent contractors. In nearly all states the employer pays the entire premium and may not deduct any of it from employee wages (Washington is a notable exception with an employee share).
Georgia requires workers' compensation coverage for any employer that regularly employs 3 or more employees, counting part-time workers.

facts.source: Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation rules
facts.fact: To self-insure workers' compensation in Georgia, an employer applies to the State Board of Workers' Compensation with three years of audited financial statements and an application fee (reported as $500).
facts.note: Fee amount and filing requirements are state rules taken from the card and not confirmed against current Board rules.

facts.fact: A Georgia employer that fails to carry required workers' compensation coverage can face civil penalties (reported as up to $5,000) and may be charged with a misdemeanor.
facts.note: Penalty amount from the card; not confirmed against the current Georgia statute.

facts.fact: Georgia employers must post a panel of physicians from which injured workers choose a treating doctor; the standard panel lists at least six providers, including an orthopedic surgeon, and a conformed panel has its own composition rules.
facts.note: Card asks which specialty a conformed panel need not include (answer ENT). Panel composition rules were not confirmed against the current statute and Board rules.

facts.fact: The cards say knowingly making false or misleading statements to get or deny Georgia workers' compensation benefits can bring civil penalties of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation and up to 12 months in prison.
facts.note: State-specific penalty figures; confirm current amounts in the Georgia Workers' Compensation Act.

facts.fact: Georgia workers' compensation defines 'catastrophic injury' to include injuries such as spinal cord injury with paralysis, amputation, severe brain injury, serious burns and total blindness; complete hearing loss in one ear does not qualify. The cards say occupational hearing loss averaging 92 decibels or more across the four test frequencies counts as total (100%) compensable hearing loss.
facts.note: State-specific; confirm the list of catastrophic injuries and the hearing-loss formula against the current statute.

facts.fact: On federal construction contracts covered by the Miller Act, the payment bond must equal 100% of the original contract price unless the contracting officer finds that impractical, so a $5.1 million contract needs a $5.1 million payment bond.
facts.note: Cards claim $2.5 million on a $5.1M contract and 40% ($1,040,000) on a $2.6M contract. Those are the pre-1999 tiered amounts; the 1999 amendments set the payment bond at 100% of contract value.

facts.fact: A bid bond assures the owner that the bidder bid in good faith and, if awarded, will sign the contract and provide the required performance and payment bonds; otherwise the surety pays damages up to the bond amount.

The Miller Act, enacted in 1935, requires performance and payment bonds on federal construction contracts (currently those over $150,000 under the FAR), because liens cannot be filed against federal property.
On federal construction projects, the performance bond is normally 100% of the original contract price.
A business owner's policy (BOP) packages commercial property and general liability coverage into one policy, usually for smaller businesses.
Umbrella liability insurance pays claims above the limits of underlying policies such as general liability, auto liability and employer's liability.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: risk management and insurance
facts.fact: Insurance transfers the financial risk of losses such as accidents, theft, and property damage from the business to an insurer in return for a premium; property insurance in particular pays for physical loss or damage to owned buildings, contents and equipment.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: insurance (inland marine)
facts.fact: A contractor's equipment floater is an inland marine policy that covers direct physical loss to mobile tools and equipment wherever they are, whether in storage, in transit, or at a jobsite.
The employer pays workers' compensation insurance premiums and, in nearly all states, may not deduct them from employees' wages.

facts.source: IRS: Do You Need a New EIN?
facts.fact: A person who buys an existing business and operates it as their own (for example as a sole proprietorship or a newly formed entity) generally must obtain a new Employer Identification Number; the seller's EIN does not transfer to the buyer.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: business organization
facts.fact: A sole proprietorship is the simplest business structure to set up, but its major drawback is that the owner has unlimited personal liability for all business debts and obligations.

A general partnership is an association of two or more persons carrying on a business for profit as co-owners. Partners should put their arrangement in a written partnership agreement, and each general partner is bound by the acts of another partner done in the name of the business.

General partners are jointly and severally liable for partnership debts. If the partnership's assets cannot cover a debt, a creditor can collect the full unpaid amount from any one general partner, who can then seek contribution from the other partners.
facts.note: Under RUPA 307, a creditor generally must first get a judgment against the partnership and exhaust partnership assets before going after a partner's personal assets.
facts.reviewed: Joint and several liability for all partnership debts comes from RUPA 306, not the original UPA. RUPA 307 also generally requires creditors to exhaust partnership assets first

facts.fact: In a limited partnership, limited partners take no part in management decisions and their liability is restricted to the amount they invested; at least one general partner manages the business and carries unlimited liability.

A partnership, LLC or corporation formed in another state is a 'foreign' entity in your state and must register (typically by filing an application for registration or certificate of authority with the Secretary of State) before doing business there.

A C corporation's main disadvantage is double taxation: profits are taxed at the corporate level and again when paid to shareholders as dividends. Its main advantage is that shareholders are generally not personally liable for corporate debts and acts.
An eligible corporation elects S corporation status by filing IRS Form 2553 (Election by a Small Business Corporation).

An S corporation avoids double taxation because its income, losses and credits pass through to shareholders, who pay tax on their share of the corporation's income whether or not that income is actually distributed; the S corporation itself generally pays no federal income tax.
facts.note: Card says an S corp pays taxes only on income distributed to members. Pass-through income is taxed to shareholders on their pro-rata share whether or not it is distributed, and the entity generally pays no federal income tax; 'members' is LLC terminology.

facts.source: IRS: Limited Liability Company (LLC); Treas. Reg. 301.7701-3
facts.fact: A limited liability company (LLC) gives its members liability protection, and by default a multi-member LLC is taxed as a partnership (single-member as a disregarded entity), so members pay federal income tax on their share of profits whether or not those profits are distributed. An LLC may instead elect to be taxed as a corporation.
facts.note: Card calls it a 'Limited Liability Corporation' and says federal income tax is filed only on income distributed to members. The correct name is limited liability company, and pass-through profits are taxed to members on their distributive share regardless of distribution.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: business organization
facts.fact: A joint venture is a business arrangement in which two or more companies combine resources to undertake a specific project, usually ending when that project is complete.

A sole proprietor who operates under any name other than their own legal name generally must file a fictitious (assumed) business name certificate, often called a DBA, with the county or state office designated by state law.
The name of a corporation, LLC or limited partnership is reserved and registered through the state's Secretary of State (or equivalent business filing office).
The main purpose of contractor licensing is to protect the health, safety and welfare of the public.

facts.source: O.C.G.A. Title 43, Chapter 41 (State Licensing Board for Residential and General Contractors)
facts.fact: Georgia's State Licensing Board for Residential and General Contractors has a residential division and a general contractor division; board members are appointed by the Governor. The card set states each division has 7 members serving 5-year terms.
facts.note: Appointment by the Governor is consistent with O.C.G.A. 43-41-3, but the division size and term length could not be confirmed against the current statute.

facts.fact: Georgia requires a residential or general contractor license for work whose total value exceeds $2,500; the card set also says residential contractors must give a written 1-year warranty on jobs over $2,500.
facts.note: The $2,500 threshold matches the commonly cited Georgia exemption, but the threshold and the written-warranty requirement were not confirmed against the current statute.

facts.source: Georgia State Licensing Board for Residential and General Contractors rules
facts.fact: Georgia contractor licenses are renewed every 2 years; the card set states continuing education of at least 3 hours for Residential-Basic and 6 hours for Residential-Light licensees, revocation if not renewed within 6 months of expiration, and a minimum $500 fine for unlicensed contracting.
facts.note: Renewal cycle, CE hours, lapse period and fine amounts are state board rules that could not be confirmed against current Georgia law.

facts.source: IRS EIN guidance; Form SS-4 instructions
facts.fact: The IRS issues Employer Identification Numbers (EINs) free of charge. A sole proprietor or single-member LLC with no employees (and no excise-tax or pension-plan filings) can use the owner's SSN, but must get an EIN once it hires employees. Corporations and partnerships always need one.
facts.note: Card says sole proprietors and single-owner LLCs do not need an EIN. That is true only if they have no employees and no excise or pension filings; hiring even one employee requires an EIN.

facts.source: O.C.G.A. 43-41 (Georgia residential and general contractor licensing)
facts.fact: In Georgia, the qualifying agent named on a business's contractor license is legally responsible for supervising, directing, managing and controlling the construction work on permits pulled under that license. The qualifying agent is jointly and equally responsible with the business for its compliance, including financial mismanagement, even if not an owner.
facts.note: State-specific licensing rule; confirm the current wording of O.C.G.A. 43-41 and the board rules.

facts.fact: Georgia's State Licensing Board for Residential and General Contractors has two divisions, residential and general contractor. The Governor appoints members to five-year terms, at least two general-contractor-division members must be small-volume builders (under $5,000,000 a year), each division meets about six times a year, and the division director may issue subpoenas.
facts.note: State-specific board structure from the cards (residential division 8 members, GC division 7, quorum 8 with at least 3 from each division, 4 residential members for residential-only actions). Membership numbers and meeting requirements have been amended over time; confirm against the current statute.

facts.fact: Georgia contractor license applicants must be at least 21. The cards say residential licensing needs about 2 years of experience and general contractor licensing about 4 years, though education can substitute for part of the experience.
facts.note: State-specific; experience and education combinations differ by license tier (residential basic, residential light commercial, general, limited tier). Confirm with the current board rules.

facts.fact: According to the cards, a licensed Georgia business must report changes to the board within set deadlines: 30 days for qualifying-agent changes, insurance changes and legal name changes, and 45 days for changes to application information or going out of business. It has 120 days to replace a departed qualifying agent before it must stop work.
facts.note: State-specific; the cards give 30 days and 45 days for similar 'changes', which suggests some confusion. Confirm each deadline against the current statute and rules.

facts.fact: In Georgia, a joint venture is treated as a separate organization that must hold its own contractor license, and the cards say each member must be licensed before the venture is formed. The cards also say a qualifying agent may serve more than one licensed business.
facts.note: State-specific. Whether one person may qualify multiple companies, and on what conditions, should be checked against the current statute and board rules.

facts.fact: The Georgia board may issue a stop-work order when it has probable cause that unlicensed work is being done, and may impose administrative fines (cards say up to $5,000 per violation). Revoking or denying a license takes a majority vote, and falsely representing work as bonded can lead to license revocation.
facts.note: State-specific enforcement provisions; confirm fine amounts and procedures against the current statute.

facts.fact: The cards say Georgia treats misrepresenting the value or percentage of completed work as a crime (fine of at least $500 and/or about three months' imprisonment), and that a building official who knowingly issues a permit to an unlicensed contractor commits a misdemeanor (fine up to $500).
facts.note: State-specific criminal penalties from the cards; confirm against the current statute.

facts.fact: In Georgia, if a licensed contractor dies leaving work unfinished, an affiliated person such as a partner, employee or relative may complete the job and must notify the board within 30 days. Abandoning a contracted project, which the cards say means 90 days without work, is grounds for discipline.
facts.note: State-specific; confirm current provisions.

facts.fact: Georgia licensing exemptions in the cards include an owner building on their own property, who after selling must wait 24 months before building another structure without a license, and minor repair work when the owner is told the worker is unlicensed.
facts.note: State-specific and likely oversimplified. Georgia also exempts small jobs below a dollar threshold, and the repair exemption has conditions. Confirm against the current statute.

facts.fact: The cards say a Georgia plumbing (specialty) contractor may do incidental electrical work on a job such as a bathroom remodel if the electrical portion is no more than $10,000 or 25% of the job, whichever is greater.
facts.note: The card is unusual and may be garbled. Trade licensing for electrical work in Georgia falls under a separate board. Confirm before relying on it.

facts.source: Georgia board rules (limited tier general contractor)
facts.fact: The cards say Georgia's limited-tier general contractor license requires a minimum net worth of $25,000 and limits each contract to $1,000,000.
facts.note: State-specific financial thresholds that may have changed; confirm current tier limits and net worth requirements with the board.

facts.source: IRS guidance: Do you need an EIN?
facts.fact: A sole proprietor or single-member LLC may use the owner's SSN instead of an EIN only if it has no employees and does not file excise, employment or pension plan returns; once it hires employees it needs an EIN.
facts.note: Card says sole proprietors and single-owner LLCs do not need an EIN, without the condition. They need one as soon as they have employees or certain filing obligations.

facts.source: IRS guidance: Do you need a new EIN?
facts.fact: A new owner who buys an existing business generally must get a new EIN; the seller's EIN cannot simply be taken over.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: business planning
facts.fact: A business plan serves three main purposes: it is a planning tool for running the company, a document presented to lenders or investors to obtain financing, and a benchmark for measuring actual performance against goals. Project contract documents are not part of a business plan.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: management and ethics
facts.fact: Effective delegation means assigning authority along with clear expectations and then following up with feedback and guidance; a written code of conduct helps establish ethical practices throughout the company.

facts.source: U.S. Small Business Administration programs (8(a), WOSB, HUBZone); USDOT DBE program
facts.fact: The Small Business Administration (SBA) provides training, counseling, loan guarantees and contracting assistance for small businesses, and government programs certify small, minority-owned and women-owned businesses (e.g., SBA 8(a), WOSB, DBE) to give them added opportunities on federal and state contracts.
A flow-down clause in a subcontract binds the subcontractor to the same obligations toward the general contractor that the general contractor owes the owner under the prime contract.

facts.source: State mechanics' lien statutes (payment and lien discharge bonds)
facts.fact: Liens by subcontractors and suppliers can be limited with surety bonds: a payment bond gives unpaid claimants a claim against the bond, and a lien discharge (release) bond can be posted to free the property from a filed lien. Procedures and effect vary by state.

Project documents include the agreement, general and supplementary conditions, drawings, specifications, addenda and modifications, along with any required bonds. The specifications describe the type and quality of materials and workmanship, while the drawings show location, dimensions and arrangement.

A contract is a legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties. A valid contract requires offer and acceptance (mutual agreement), consideration (something of value exchanged, not necessarily money), competent parties with legal capacity, and a legal purpose. A written contract helps prevent disputes.
Acceptance is unconditional agreement to the terms of an offer, often shown by signing it. A counteroffer is not acceptance; it rejects the original offer and becomes a new offer.

Progress payments are partial payments made during construction based on the percentage of work completed (usually measured against a schedule of values) or on completion of defined phases. Under AIA A201 the architect reviews the contractor's payment application and certifies to the owner the amount due, and also certifies substantial completion.

Retainage is a percentage (commonly 5% to 10%) withheld from each progress payment and released after completion; it gives the owner leverage to ensure the work is finished and protection against unpaid subcontractor and supplier liens. Many states cap retainage on public and some private work.

On a $200,000 lump-sum contract with 10% retainage, when the work is 90% complete the contractor has earned $180,000 but been paid only $162,000 ($18,000 retained); the remaining balance is $38,000 ($20,000 of unfinished work plus $18,000 retainage).
facts.note: Card answers $20,000, which ignores the $18,000 retainage withheld from the 90% earned. With 10% retainage, the payments made total $162,000, so $38,000 remains.

facts.fact: Responsibility for permits is set by the contract. Under AIA A201-2017, unless the contract says otherwise, the contractor secures and pays for the building permit and the permits, fees and licenses needed for the work, while the owner secures and pays for approvals, easements, assessments and charges such as zoning or utility connection approvals.
facts.note: Cards say the owner is responsible for purchasing and paying for all permits. Under the standard AIA A201 general conditions the contractor obtains and pays for the building permit; the owner handles approvals and easements. Local law also often requires the licensed contractor to pull the permit.

facts.fact: A breach of contract is a party's failure to perform its obligations without legal excuse. A material breach goes to the heart of the contract and justifies termination; an immaterial (minor) breach, such as a progress payment one day late, entitles the other party only to damages. A contractor who walks off the job permanently over such a minor delay commits a material breach itself.

Contract breaches are classed as material or immaterial (minor). A material breach defeats the essential purpose of the contract and lets the other party stop performing, terminate and sue for damages; an immaterial breach only entitles the other party to damages while the contract continues.

Liquidated damages are a dollar amount agreed in the contract in advance (for example a set sum per calendar day of late completion) that the contractor pays the owner for delay. Courts enforce them only if they are a reasonable estimate of hard-to-calculate actual damages, not a penalty.

In contract law, 'damages' is the money awarded to compensate a party for the loss it suffered because of the other party's breach. Common types are compensatory (actual), consequential, liquidated and nominal damages; punitive damages are rarely available for a pure breach of contract.

facts.source: AIA A201 general conditions; CSI project manual Division 00
facts.fact: The standard general conditions of a construction contract are modified or added to for a particular project through supplementary (supplemental) conditions, which are issued with the bid documents so bidders price the changes.

An indemnification (hold-harmless) clause obligates one party (the indemnitor) to cover the other party's (the indemnitee's) losses, defense costs or liability, typically for claims brought by third parties. Many states have anti-indemnity statutes that void clauses requiring a party to be indemnified for its own sole negligence.

The warranty (guarantee) provisions of a contract define the contractor's duty to repair defective work after completion and give the owner the right to demand correction. Under AIA A201 the contractor must correct nonconforming work discovered within one year after substantial completion, in addition to any longer express warranties.

facts.source: Contract law fundamentals; NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: contract types
facts.fact: A lump-sum (stipulated-sum) contract fixes one total price for the whole scope, so the contractor carries the risk of cost overruns and the owner is best protected from unexpected costs. It should only be used when complete, detailed plans and specifications allow an accurate estimate.

facts.source: Contract law fundamentals; NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: contract types
facts.fact: Under a cost-plus contract the owner reimburses the contractor's actual costs of labor, materials and other job costs plus a fee (fixed amount or percentage) for overhead and profit; the owner carries most of the cost risk unless a guaranteed maximum price (GMP) is added.

facts.source: Contract law fundamentals; NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: contract types
facts.fact: A unit-price contract pays a set price per unit of work (per cubic yard, linear foot, ton, etc.) times the actual measured quantity, and is used when the full quantity of work cannot be determined in advance, such as excavation or paving. Unit-price or cost-plus contracts suit jobs without detailed plans.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project delivery methods
facts.fact: In design-build delivery a single entity contracts with the owner to provide both design and construction, giving the owner one point of responsibility. Turnkey delivery is the closest relative: the contractor handles design and construction and may also arrange land or financing, handing over a ready-to-use facility.

Addenda are written changes to the bidding documents issued before bids are opened or the contract is signed; changes after award are made by change order. A change order must be in writing and signed by the owner and contractor (and the architect under AIA A201), and it may add, delete or alter work and adjust the contract sum and/or contract time.

An allowance is a placeholder amount in the contract for an item not yet selected. If the owner's selection costs more (or less) than the allowance, the contract sum is adjusted by a written change order.

Contract claims procedures give owner and contractor a path to resolve disputes over extra money or time arising from changes. Under AIA A201 a claim goes first to the Initial Decision Maker (the architect unless another person is named), then to mediation, then to binding dispute resolution such as arbitration or litigation.

After a bid is accepted, contracts usually allow a product substitution only for limited reasons, such as the specified item being discontinued or unavailable, and only with the architect's or owner's written approval.
facts.note: Allowed grounds for substitution depend on each project's specifications; 'discontinued product' is a typical but not universal ground.

facts.fact: In mediation a neutral mediator helps the parties negotiate, but the parties decide whether and on what terms to settle; it is non-binding unless they sign an agreement. In arbitration a neutral arbitrator hears the case and issues an award that is legally binding on the parties.

facts.source: CSI MasterFormat Division 00 (procurement and contracting requirements)
facts.fact: In a typical project manual, Division 00 holds the procurement (bidding) requirements, such as the invitation to bid, instructions to bidders, bid forms and addenda, and the contracting requirements, such as the agreement, bonds, general and supplementary conditions and change order forms.

Oral contracts are generally legally enforceable but unwise, because their terms are hard to prove. The statute of frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing, including those for interests in real estate, those that cannot be performed within one year, and sales of goods of $500 or more under UCC 2-201; many states also require written home-improvement contracts.

Under the parol evidence rule, a final, fully integrated written contract cannot be contradicted by earlier or simultaneous oral agreements, so the written terms control. Later modifications, including some oral ones, can still change the contract unless the contract or a statute requires changes to be in writing.
facts.note: Card says written agreements 'always' take precedence over oral agreements. That holds for prior or contemporaneous oral terms under the parol evidence rule, but a later oral modification can be valid in some situations, so 'always' overstates it.

facts.fact: When contract language is ambiguous and the ambiguity cannot be resolved, courts interpret it against the party that drafted the contract (the rule of contra proferentem).

A subcontract should identify at least the project name and location, the scope of work, the contract price, the payment schedule and retainage, and should also address schedule, insurance, indemnity and change-order procedures.

In a cost-plus contract, the owner pays the contractor's actual allowable costs plus an agreed fee (fixed or a percentage). Payment is not based on a percentage of work completed against a fixed price.

Under the federal Prompt Payment Act, a federal agency must pay construction progress payments within 14 days after receiving a proper payment request, and final payment (including retainage) generally within 30 days. Late payments earn interest.

On federal construction contracts, the prime contractor must pay each subcontractor for satisfactory work within 7 days after receiving payment from the government. Otherwise it owes the sub an interest penalty.
A construction (mechanic's) lien is a claim against the improved real property. It secures payment for contractors, subcontractors, laborers and suppliers who improved the property and were not paid.

In lien law, the 'contractor' is the party in direct contract (privity) with the property owner, usually the general contractor. Subcontractors and suppliers below the GC are not in privity with the owner and generally must give extra notices to protect lien rights.

In many states, paying the general contractor in full does not by itself protect the owner from liens by unpaid subcontractors and suppliers, who can lien the property directly. Owners protect themselves by getting lien waivers or releases from everyone who furnished labor or materials before or as they pay.
In Georgia, a lien claim must be filed for record within 90 days after the claimant last furnished labor, services or materials to the property.
facts.note: State-specific lien law. The 90-day period matches O.C.G.A. 44-14-361.1 as amended in 2020 (effective 2021), but confirm against the current statute.

facts.fact: In Georgia, a lien claimant must start a lawsuit to enforce the lien within 365 days after the lien claim is filed, or the lien expires.
facts.note: One card measures 365 days from when the claim comes due (the pre-2021 rule); another measures from filing. The 2020 amendments (SB 315) moved the start to the filing date. Confirm against the current statute.

facts.fact: In Georgia, after filing a lien claim, the claimant must send a true copy to the property owner (and to the contractor where required) within 2 business days of filing.
facts.note: State-specific lien law; confirm the current notice recipients and the 2-business-day deadline against the statute.

facts.fact: In Georgia, a lien claimant must also file a notice of commencement of the lien enforcement action with the clerk of superior court. If no such notice is filed within 395 days of the date the lien claim was filed, the lien may be disregarded.
facts.note: State-specific lien law (the notice is generally due within 30 days of filing suit, with an outside limit of 395 days from the lien filing). Confirm against the current statute.

facts.fact: On Georgia private projects, the owner or contractor files a Notice of Commencement with the clerk of superior court in the county where the property is located, no later than 15 days after the contractor physically starts work.
facts.note: State-specific; confirm the 15-day deadline and the required contents against the current statute.

facts.fact: In Georgia, a subcontractor or supplier not in privity with the contractor must send a Notice to Contractor within 30 days of first furnishing labor or materials or within 30 days of the Notice of Commencement being filed, whichever is later, to preserve lien rights when a Notice of Commencement has been filed.
facts.note: Card says 30 days of 'receiving' the notice of commencement. The statute is generally read as the later of first furnishing or the filing of the Notice of Commencement. Confirm the current wording.

facts.fact: Under older Georgia law, a supplier who kept an improper preliminary notice of lien rights on record after being paid and asked to cancel it could be held liable for the owner's attorney's fees to remove it.
facts.note: Card says the supplier pays the owner's $2,500 attorney fee. The 2020 lien-law amendments (effective 2021) eliminated the preliminary notice of lien rights, so this scenario may be outdated. Confirm against current law.

facts.fact: Under the Georgia Prompt Pay Act, the cards say an owner must pay the contractor within 15 days of receiving a payment request for completed work, and late payments carry interest of 1% per month. The cards also say the Act does not apply to improvements of fewer than 12 residential units.
facts.note: State-specific; confirm payment deadlines (including the contractor-to-sub deadline), the interest rate and the residential exclusion against the current statute.

facts.fact: The cards say that in Georgia, once a subcontractor's work is 50% complete and the contractor is being paid retainage, the sub becomes entitled to its share of that retainage.
facts.note: The card is muddled. Georgia limits retainage (commonly 10% until 50% completion, then no further retainage if work is satisfactory). Confirm how release to subcontractors works under the current statute.

facts.source: Contract law fundamentals; statute of frauds
facts.fact: Oral contracts can be binding but are discouraged because their terms are hard to prove in a dispute, and some contracts (e.g. real estate or those not performable within a year) must be in writing under the statute of frauds.
A valid contract is an agreement between two or more parties with legal capacity, with offer and acceptance (mutual assent), consideration and a lawful purpose.
Under AIA-based contracts, the architect reviews the contractor's application for payment and certifies to the owner the amount due based on work completed before a progress payment is made.

facts.source: AIA A201 Article 7 (changes in the work)
facts.fact: A change order is a written instrument, signed by owner, contractor and architect, that adds to, deletes from or alters the contract work and may adjust the contract sum and contract time.
In mediation a neutral helps the parties reach their own voluntary settlement; in arbitration a neutral third party hears the case and issues a decision that is usually binding on the parties.
A flow-down clause binds the subcontractor to the general contractor the same way the general contractor is bound to the owner under the prime contract.

Under AIA A201, unless the contract documents say otherwise, the contractor obtains and pays for the building permit and other government permits, fees, licenses and inspections needed to complete the work.
facts.note: Card says the owner is responsible for purchasing permits. Under the standard AIA A201 general conditions the contractor secures and pays for permits unless the contract assigns them elsewhere; responsibility is set by the contract.

facts.source: Contract law fundamentals (material vs. minor breach)
facts.fact: A minor breach, such as a payment that is one day late, lets the injured party recover damages but not stop performing. Walking off the job for good in response is itself a material breach, and a contract should be terminated only for a material breach.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: contract types
facts.fact: Under a cost-plus contract, the monthly pay application bills the owner for the actual costs incurred, documented by records, plus the agreed fee, rather than a percentage of a fixed lump sum.

NEPA applies to major federal actions, meaning projects that are federally funded, federally permitted or on federal land. These require an environmental review (categorical exclusion, environmental assessment or environmental impact statement) before proceeding. The EPA is the federal agency charged with protecting human health and air, water and land quality.

facts.source: Clean Air Act; 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F
facts.fact: The main air-quality issues on construction sites are open burning, dust and engine emissions, and ozone-depleting refrigerants such as CFCs, which may not be vented and must be handled by certified technicians. Watering exposed soil and haul roads is the basic way to control dust and avoid violations.

Before any demolition or renovation, the owner or operator must have the building thoroughly inspected for asbestos. Written notice must be sent to EPA or the delegated state agency at least 10 working days before any demolition, and before renovations disturbing regulated asbestos above the threshold amounts (260 linear ft, 160 sq ft or 35 cu ft).

The Clean Water Act prohibits discharging any pollutant into waters of the United States without a permit, such as an NPDES permit. Sediment from eroding construction sites is a major source of water pollution, and a site can send more sediment into streams in a short time than natural processes deposit over decades.

NPDES stormwater permit coverage is required for construction that disturbs 1 acre or more of land, or less than 1 acre if it is part of a larger common plan of development disturbing 1 acre or more. Coverage requires a stormwater pollution prevention plan (SWPPP).

Ordinary construction and demolition debris such as scrap wood, drywall, brick and concrete is generally non-hazardous solid waste. Used oil (40 CFR 279) and batteries (universal waste, 40 CFR 273) must be kept out of regular debris and managed under their own rules.
